Symmetric powers: structure, smoothability, and applications

Cosimo Flavi, Joachim Jelisiejew, Mateusz Michałek Address: (Cosimo Flavi) Wydział Matematyki, Informatyki i Mechaniki, Uniwersytet Warszawski, ul. Stefana Banacha 2, 02-097 Warsaw, Poland. Email address: c.flavi@uw.edu.pl Address: (Joachim Jelisiejew) Wydział Matematyki, Informatyki i Mechaniki, Uniwersytet Warszawski, ul. Stefana Banacha 2, 02-097 Warsaw, Poland. Email address: j.jelisiejew@uw.edu.pl Address: (Mateusz Michałek) Fachbereich Mathematik und Statistik, Universität Konstanz, Fach D 197 D-78457, Konstanz, Germany. Email address: mateusz.michalek@uni-konstanz.de
Abstract.

We investigate border ranks of twisted powers of polynomials and smoothability of symmetric powers of algebras. We prove that the latter are smoothable. For the former, we obtain upper bounds for the border rank in general and prove that they are optimal under mild conditions. We give applications to complexity theory. Many of the results rest on the notion of an encompassing polynomial, which we introduce.

Key words and phrases:
Additive decompositions, apolar algebra, border rank, secant varieties, smoothable rank, symmetric tensor, tensor rank
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 15A69; Secondary 14N07.

1. Introduction

We study two classical and challenging problems in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra: the classification of smoothable finite algebras, and the classification of homogeneous polynomials of small border rank. Both problems are widely regarded as very difficult, primarily due to the vast diversity of possible examples and lack of general structure theorems.

Nevertheless, significant progress has been made in particular cases. Notable examples include subschemes of 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} [43], Gorenstein subschemes of 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} [61], and homogeneous forms in a small number of variables [66]. Additional constructions involve subschemes defined by monomial ideals or complete intersections, as well as explicit constructions derived via computational methods such as limits of families of points and linear combinations of powers of forms.

Outside these specific instances, one of the few general techniques applicable to both smoothability and border rank involves the use of tensor powers. This method yields the following two key properties:

  1. (1)

    if AA is a smoothable algebra, then for every dd the tensor product A⊗dA^{\otimes d} is smoothable;

  2. (2)

    if F=F⁡(x0,…,xn)F=F(x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}) is a homogeneous polynomial of border rank at most rr, then for every dd the polynomial

    F⊗d:=F(x1,0,…,x1,n)F(x2,0,…,x2,n)⋯F(xd,0,…,xd,n)F^{\otimes d}:=F(x_{1,0},\ldots,x_{1,n})F(x_{2,0},\ldots,x_{2,n})\cdots F(x_{d,0},\ldots,x_{d,n})

    in (n+1)​d(n+1)d variables has border rank with respect to the Segre-Veronese variety (=variety of monomials of the same multi-degree as F⊗dF^{\otimes d}) at most rdr^{d}.

In this article we provide twisted symmetric power analogues of the two results, see subsection 1.1 and subsection 1.2 below. Both results are special cases of more general structure theorems, which we explain below. The passage from tensor to symmetric powers may seem to be automatic, but it is not, in fact it is unexpectedly subtle, see Counterexamples 1.1, 1.2, 5.1 below and the discussion about the necessity of twisting. In fact, while the tensor powers are a classical tool, it seems that almost nothing is known about symmetric powers.

Smoothability is of great interest for moduli spaces, with applications to enumerative geometry and combinatorics. Border rank is central to the classical theory of secant varieties (see [7, 8, 27]), with applications to statistics, signal processing (see [30, 37, 68]) and, expecially, to complexity theory and the geometry of tensors ([25, 64, 35]). From this point of view, it is important to look at the asymptotical behavior: to consider sequences of polynomials or algebras with increasing degree and number of variables. In this aspect, the gain from passing from tensor to symmetric powers is very notable. Also in the symmetric power setting the rank we consider is always the usual Waring rank, in contrast to the right hand side of (2) above, where it changes to the Segre-Veronese rank.

1.1. Smoothability

The situation is much cleaner for smoothability, so we begin with this part. We talk about finite schemes Z=Spec⁡(A)Z=\Spec(A) rather than algebras AA. By Ap⁡(−)\Ap(-) we denote the apolar algebra.

Theorem 1.0.
  1. (1)

    For every finite smoothable scheme ZZ, its dd-th symmetric power Sd​ZS^{d}Z is smoothable for every d≥1d\geq 1;

  2. (2)

    if f∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] and d≥1d\geq 1 are such that

    dim𝕂Ap⁡(fd)=(dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)+d−1d),\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f^{d})=\binom{\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f)+d-1}{d},

    then the scheme

    Zd=Spec⁡(Ap⁡(fd))Z_{d}=\Spec\bigl(\Ap(f^{d})\bigr)

    is isomorphic to Sd​Z1S^{d}Z_{1}. In particular, if Z1Z_{1} is smoothable, then ZdZ_{d} is smoothable.

Note that in general the smoothability of Spec⁡(Ap⁡(f))\Spec\bigl(\Ap(f)\bigr) does not imply the smoothability of Spec⁡(Ap⁡(fd))\Spec\bigl(\Ap(f^{d})\bigr) for d≥1d\geq 1. In subsection 5.1 we provide an ff such that Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) is smoothable, while Ap⁡(f2)\Ap(f^{2}) is not. The proof of subsection 1.1 is based on the following abstract but useful proposition.

Proposition 1.0.

Let ZZ be a finite scheme with an action of a linearly reductive algebraic group GG and suppose that ZZ admits a GG-equivariant smoothing 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Then 𝒵/⁣/G\mathcal{Z}\mathbin{\mathchoice{\left/\mkern-6.0mu\right/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}}G is a smoothing of Z/⁣/GZ\mathbin{\mathchoice{\left/\mkern-6.0mu\right/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}}G, so Z/⁣/GZ\mathbin{\mathchoice{\left/\mkern-6.0mu\right/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}}G is smoothable.

For the case Spec⁡(Ap⁡(fd))\Spec\bigl(\Ap(f^{d})\bigr), we have Z=Spec⁡(Ap⁡(f)⊗d)Z=\Spec\bigl(\Ap(f)^{\otimes d}\bigr) and G=ΣdG=\Sigma_{d} is the symmetric group acting on ZZ by permuting the copies of Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f). subsection 1.1 applies in other natural situations, notably for the Veronese subalgebras. We discuss these now.

Example 1.0.

Fix an arbitrary dd and consider the monomial algebra

A⁡(d)≔𝕂⁡[α1,…,αd](α12,…,αd2){A(d)}\coloneqq\frac{\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d}]}{(\alpha_{1}^{2},\ldots,\alpha_{d}^{2})}

and the corresponding scheme Zd≔Spec⁡(A⁡(d))Z_{d}\coloneqq\Spec({A(d)}). Let G≔⟨g⟩G\coloneqq\langle g\rangle be a cyclic group of order two that acts on

Z1=Spec⁡(𝕂⁡[α]/(α2))Z_{1}=\Spec\bigl(\mathbb{K}[\alpha]/(\alpha^{2})\bigr)

by g⋅α≔−αg\cdot\alpha\coloneqq-\alpha. The scheme Z1Z_{1} has a GG-equivariant smoothing 𝕂⁡[α,t]/(α2−t)\mathbb{K}[\alpha,t]/(\alpha^{2}-t). Therefore, also the scheme Zd=Z1×⋯×Z1Z_{d}=Z_{1}\times\cdots\times Z_{1} admits a GG-equivariant smoothing, so

Zd/⁣/G≃Spec⁡(A​(d)ℤ/2)Z_{d}\mathbin{\mathchoice{\left/\mkern-6.0mu\right/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}}G\simeq\Spec\bigl({A(d)}^{\mathbb{Z}/2}\bigr)

is smoothable.

subsection 1.1is sharp in that the assumption of the existence of GG-equivariant smoothing is necessary, as we show in the following example.

Example 1.0.

Let us consider the monomial algebra

A≔𝕂⁡[α1,…,α9](α12,…,α92)A\coloneqq\frac{\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{9}]}{(\alpha_{1}^{2},\ldots,\alpha_{9}^{2})}

which has degree 512512 and Hilbert function

HFA=(1,9,36,84,126,126,84,36,9,1).\HF_{A}=(1,9,36,84,126,126,84,36,9,1).

The corresponding subscheme Z≔Spec⁡(A)⊆𝔸9Z\coloneqq\Spec(A)\subseteq\mathbb{A}^{9} is torus-fixed and in particular the cyclic group G≔ℤ/3G\coloneqq\mathbb{Z}/3 acts on it by multiplying each variable by a third root of unity. In this case

Z/⁣/G≃Spec⁡(Aℤ/3)=Spec⁡(𝕂⊕A3⊕A6⊕A9).Z\mathbin{\mathchoice{\left/\mkern-6.0mu\right/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}}G\simeq\Spec\bigl(A^{\mathbb{Z}/3}\bigr)=\Spec\left(\mathbb{K}\oplus A_{3}\oplus A_{6}\oplus A_{9}\right).

This is a subscheme with Hilbert function (1,84,84,1)(1,84,84,1), which is not smoothable by the criterion of [59]*Theorem 1.2.

Let us define a more general class of algebras which includes the last two examples.

Definition 1.1.

Given a graded algebra A=⨁i≥0AiA=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}A_{i} and a positive integer kk the algebra ⨁i≥0Ak​i\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}A_{ki} is called the kk-th Veronese subalgebra.

The previous examples, as well as our theorems on passing to symmetric powers, can be seen as specific cases of a more general question:

Question 1.1.

Given a finite smoothable scheme Spec⁡(A)\Spec(A) with an action of a group GG, when is Spec⁡(AG)\Spec(A^{G}) also smoothable?

As we can see in subsection 1.1 the answer is not always positive. Still, subsection 1.1 and subsection 1.1 provide many examples when it is.

1.2. Powers of polynomials and their ranks

We now shift our attention from smoothability to border rank. Let F∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn]F\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}] be a homogeneous polynomial. One can mimic (2) above as follows: replace rd=dim𝕂(𝕂r)⊗dr^{d}=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}(\mathbb{K}^{r})^{\otimes d} with (r+d−1d)=dim𝕂Sd​(𝕂r)\binom{r+d-1}{d}=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}S^{d}(\mathbb{K}^{r}) and ask whether if brk⁡(F)≤r\brk(F){\leq}r, then

brk⁡(Fd)≤(r+d−1d)\brk(F^{d})\leq\binom{r+d-1}{d}

for all d≥1d\geq 1. However, this inequality is false even in the simplest cases.

Example 1.1.

Let

F≔x03+x13∈𝕂⁡[x0,x1].F\coloneqq x_{0}^{3}+x_{1}^{3}\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},x_{1}].

Then rk⁡(F)=2\rk(F)=2 and the middle catalecticant rank of F2F^{2} is 4>(32)4>\binom{3}{2}, so brk⁡(F2)≥4\brk(F^{2})\geq 4, in fact brk⁡(F2)=4\brk(F^{2})=4. Also brk⁡(F[2])=4\brk(F^{[2]})=4, where F[2]F^{[2]} is the divided square of FF. Similar results will be obtained for Fermat cubics in more variables, for exponents high than 33 and so on.

Since the upper bound on the border rank is false in the simplest case of two variables, it may come as a surprise that a bound can be achieved in a fairly general situation, which we explain below. We need two notions.

First, for a homogeneous polynomial F=∑iλi​𝐱i∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn]F=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{x}^{i}\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}], where i=(i0,…,in)i=(i_{0},\dots,i_{n}), we define the twist of FF by

tw⁡(F):=∑iλi​1i0!​𝐱i.\mathrm{tw}(F):=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\frac{1}{i_{0}!}\mathbf{x}^{i}.

For example,

tw⁡(x02​x1​x2+x03​x2+x14)=12​x02​x1​x2+16​x03​x2+x14.\mathrm{tw}(x_{0}^{2}x_{1}x_{2}+x_{0}^{3}x_{2}+x_{1}^{4})=\frac{1}{2}x_{0}^{2}x_{1}x_{2}+\frac{1}{6}x_{0}^{3}x_{2}+x_{1}^{4}.

The reparametrization used in the twist is unfortunately necessary below, as examples such as subsection 5.1 show. The technical reason for the need of twists is explained in §2.3 below. It would be very interesting to find a more conceptual explanation.

Second, we say that a polynomial ff is encompassing if the parts of degree ≤1\leq 1 of a basis of the space of its partials are linearly independent, see 4.1. For example, the polynomial f:-x12+x2f\coloneq x_{1}^{2}+x_{2} is encompassing, because the degree ≤1\leq 1 part of derivatives of ff are

(f)≤1=x2,∂f∂x1=(∂f∂x1)≤1=2​x1,∂2f∂x12=(∂2f∂x12)≤1=2,(f)_{\leq 1}=x_{2},\qquad\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}}=\biggl(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}}\biggr)_{\leq 1}=2x_{1},\qquad\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{1}^{2}}=\biggl(\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{1}^{2}}\biggr)_{\leq 1}=2,

and they are linearly independent. The form F:-x12+x22F\coloneq x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2} is, instead, not encompassing, because already F≤1F_{\leq 1} is zero (for this reason, homogeneous polynomials of degree ≥2\geq 2 are never encompassing). Our second theorem is as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

Let F∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn]F\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}] be a concise homogeneous polynomial such that its dehomogenization f:-F|x0=1f\coloneq F|_{x_{0}=1} is encompassing and the apolar algebra of ff is smoothable. Then, for every d≥1d\geq 1, the following conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    the form tw⁡(Fd)\mathrm{tw}(F^{d}) has smoothable rank, border rank, cactus rank, border cactus rank, and the middle catalecticant rank all equal to (n+dd)\binom{n+d}{d};

  2. (2)

    the scheme Spec⁡(Ap⁡(fd))\Spec\bigl(\Ap(f^{d})\bigr) is smoothable and apolar to tw⁡(Fd)\mathrm{tw}(F^{d}) under a suitable embedding (see §2.3).

Example 1.1.

Let QQ be a full rank quadric given by

Q:-x0​xn+x12+x22+…+xn−12.Q\coloneq x_{0}x_{n}+x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\ldots+x_{n-1}^{2}.

The dehomogenization pn:-Q|x0=1p_{n}\coloneq Q|_{x_{0}=1} is encompassing. By subsection 1.2, for every d≥1d\geq 1 the form tw⁡(Qd)\mathrm{tw}(Q^{d}) has smoothable and border ranks equal to

(n+dd).\binom{n+d}{d}.

For ternary quadratic forms and without twisting this result was obtained by the first author in [42]*Theorem 4.5. We warn that not every dehomogenization of QQ is encompassing: consider Q|∑i=0nλi​xi=1Q|_{\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}x_{i}=1}, where λi∈𝕂\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{K}. If Q⁡(λ0,…,λn)=0Q(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})=0, then, up to coordinate change, Q|∑i=0nλi​xi=1Q|_{\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}x_{i}=1} is Q|x0=1Q|_{x_{0}=1}, so it is encompassing. However, if Q⁡(λ0,…,λn)≠0Q(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\neq 0, then Q|∑i=0nλi​xi=1Q|_{\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}x_{i}=1} is, up to coordinate change, equal to 1+x12+…+xn21+x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+x_{n}^{2}, which is not encompassing. In particular, a general dehomogenization is not encompassing.

Example 1.1.

Let us consider the cubic

F:-x13+x23+⋯+xn3+x0​(x1​y1+⋯+xn​yn)+x02​y0F\coloneq x_{1}^{3}+x_{2}^{3}+\dots+x_{n}^{3}+x_{0}\left(x_{1}y_{1}+\dots+x_{n}y_{n}\right)+x_{0}^{2}y_{0}

in 2​(n+1)2(n+1) variables. The dehomogenization F|x0=1F|_{x_{0}=1} is encompassing and the apolar algebra

Ap⁡(F|x0=1)≃Ap⁡(x13+x23+…+xn3)\Ap(F|_{x_{0}=1})\simeq\Ap(x_{1}^{3}+x_{2}^{3}+\ldots+x_{n}^{3})

is smoothable, see [41, Theorem 3.3] or [58, Example 2.16] for the isomorphism. Hence, by subsection 1.2, for every d≥1d\geq 1 we have

brk⁡(tw⁡(Fd))=(2​n+d+1d).\brk\bigl(\mathrm{tw}(F^{d})\bigr)=\binom{2n+d+1}{d}.

We warn the reader that twisting is necessary: even for FF satisfying the assumptions of subsection 1.2, the border rank of both the square F2F^{2} and the divided square F[2]F^{[2]} can be higher than (n+12)\binom{n+1}{2}, see subsection 5.1.

The theorem implies that tw⁡(F)\mathrm{tw}(F) has the minimal possible border rank nn and smoothable rank also equal to nn, so tw⁡(F)\mathrm{tw}(F) is not wild in the sense of [22]. A natural question is: how limiting are the assumptions in subsection 1.2? The following theorem shows that the smoothability of Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) is the primary requirement: we may always construct an encompassing polynomial that restricts to ours by adding a minimal possible number of new variables.

We say that a polynomial G∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn]G\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}] restricts to a polynomial F∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xk]F\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{k}], where k≤nk\leq n, if F=G|xk+1=0,…,xn=0F=G|_{x_{k+1}=0,\ldots,x_{n}=0}.

Theorem 1.1.

Let F∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xk]F\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{k}] be a concise homogeneous polynomial, let f:-F|x0=1f\coloneq F|_{x_{0}=1} be its dehomogenization, and assume that Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) be smoothable. If dim𝕂(Ap⁡(f))=n\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f)\bigr)=n, then there exists a concise homogeneous polynomial G∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn]G\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}] restricting to FF and such that GG satisfies the assumptions of subsection 1.2. In particular,

brk⁡(tw⁡(Fd))≤(n+dd),\brk(\mathrm{tw}(F^{d}))\leq\binom{n+d}{d},

for every d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}. Moreover, for g:-G|x0=1g\coloneq G|_{x_{0}=1} we have Ap⁡(g)≃Ap⁡(f)\Ap(g)\simeq\Ap(f).

The proof of subsection 1.2 is constructive and the form GG is determined explicitly. Namely, let us take a concise homogeneous F∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xk]F\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{k}] and f=F|x0=1f=F|_{x_{0}=1}. The apolar algebra Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) is a quotient of the dual ring 𝒟:=𝕂⁡[α1,…,αk]\mathcal{D}:=\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}], where

αi:-∂∂xi\alpha_{i}\coloneq\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}

for every i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k. Let us consider a basis ℬ\mathcal{B} of Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) given by

ℬ:-{f,α1∘f,…,αk∘f,σ1∘f,…,σn−k−1∘f},\mathcal{B}\coloneq\{f,\alpha_{1}\circ f,\ldots,\alpha_{k}\circ f,\sigma_{1}\circ f,\ldots,\sigma_{n-k-1}\circ f\},

where σi∈𝒟≥2\sigma_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\geq 2}. For any multi-index 𝐚∈ℤ≥0n−k−1\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n-k-1}, let us define

σ𝐚:-σ1𝐚1⋯σn−k−1𝐚n−k−1and𝐲𝐚:-y1𝐚1⋯yn−k−1𝐚n−k−1.\sigma^{\mathbf{a}}\coloneq\sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{a}_{1}}\cdots\sigma_{n-k-1}^{\mathbf{a}_{n-k-1}}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathbf{y}^{\mathbf{a}}\coloneq y_{1}^{\mathbf{a}_{1}}\cdots y_{n-k-1}^{\mathbf{a}_{n-k-1}}.

Then the polynomial g∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xk,y1,…,yn−k−1]g\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{k},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n-k-1}] is defined by a Taylor-like series

(1.2) g:-∑𝐚∈ℤ≥0n−k−1𝐲𝐚𝐚!​(σ𝐚∘f)g\coloneq\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n-k-1}}\frac{\mathbf{y}^{\mathbf{a}}}{\mathbf{a}!}(\sigma^{\mathbf{a}}\circ f)

and G∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xk,y1,…,yn−k−1]G\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{k},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n-k-1}] is the homogenization of gg with respect to x0x_{0}. To obtain GG in 𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn]\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}] one takes xj:-yj−kx_{j}\coloneq y_{j-k} for j>kj>k.

Example 1.2.

To obtain subsection 1.2, let us consider the form

F:-x12+⋯+xn−12∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn−1].F\coloneq x_{1}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n-1}^{2}\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n-1}].

{1,α1,…,αn−1,σ1},\{1,\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n-1},\sigma_{1}\},

σ12∘f=σ1∘1=0,\sigma_{1}^{2}\circ f=\sigma_{1}\circ 1=0,

x12+⋯+xn−12+x0​y1,x_{1}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n-1}^{2}+x_{0}y_{1},

as expected.

Example 1.2.

To obtain subsection 1.2, let us consider the form

F:-x13+⋯+xn3∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn].F\coloneq x_{1}^{3}+\cdots+x_{n}^{3}\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}].

Then, we take f:-F|x0=1f\coloneq F|_{x_{0}=1} and as a basis of Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) fix the set

{1,α1,…,αn,σ1,…,σn,σn+1},\{1,\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n},\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{n},\sigma_{n+1}\},

with σi:-αi2/2\sigma_{i}\coloneq\alpha_{i}^{2}/2 for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n and σn+1:-α13/6\sigma_{n+1}\coloneq\alpha_{1}^{3}/6. For every i,ji,j we have σi∘(σj∘f)=0\sigma_{i}\circ(\sigma_{j}\circ f)=0, so that the formula (1.2) becomes

g=f+x1​y1+…+xn​yn+yn+1,g=f+x_{1}y_{1}+\ldots+x_{n}y_{n}+y_{n+1},

which homogenizes to the form from the example.

Having discussed the abundance of encompassing polynomials, we present a more geometric point of view for them. In the projective setting, there exist elegant classical links between the algebra of a homogeneous polynomial F∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn]F\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}] and the topology of its gradient map

grad⁡(F)=(∂F∂x0,…,∂F∂xn):ℙn⇢ℙn,\grad(F)=\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{0}},\ldots,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{n}}\right)\colon\mathbb{P}^{n}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n},

also called the polar map. For further details, the reader can see, e.g., [50, 38, 39, 51].

In the affine setting, we prove the following analogue which in particular gives a characterization of polynomials which have dominant affine gradient maps and a characterization of polynomials with maximal growth of powers. We need one definition. By section 3 for every polynomial ff with dim𝕂(Ap⁡(f))=ℓ\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f)\bigr)=\ell and every d≥1d\geq 1 we have

(1.3) dim𝕂Ap⁡(fd)≤(ℓ+d−1d).\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f^{d})\leq\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}.

We say that ff has maximal growth of powers if for every d≥1d\geq 1 equality holds in (1.3).

Theorem 1.3.

Let f∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] be a concise polynomial and take ℓ:-dim𝕂(Ap⁡(f))\ell\coloneq\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f)\bigr). Then, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    ff has maximal growth of powers;

  2. (2)

    the total gradient map

    totalGrad⁡(f)=(∂f∂𝐱𝐚1,…,∂f∂𝐱𝐚ℓ−1):𝔸n⇢𝔸ℓ−1\totalgrad(f)=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{a}_{1}}},\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{a}_{\ell-1}}}\right)\colon\mathbb{A}^{n}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{\ell-1}

    is dominant, where the set

    {∂f∂𝐱𝐚i}i∪{1}\biggl\{\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{a}_{i}}}\biggr\}_{i}\cup\{1\}

    forms a basis of the space of all partials of ff;

  3. (3)

    the partials of ff are homogeneously algebraically independent (see §4);

  4. (4)

    ff is an encompassing polynomial.

Moreover, if these conditions hold, then ℓ=n+1\ell=n+1 and the total gradient map totalGrad⁡(f)\totalgrad(f) is, up to coordinate changes, the usual gradient map

grad⁡(f)=(∂f∂x1,…,∂f∂xn):𝔸n⇢𝔸n.\grad(f)=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}},\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}\right)\colon\mathbb{A}^{n}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}.

A word of caution is that the rational map grad⁡(f)\grad(f) yields a rational map ℙn⇢ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n}, but this map is in general not equal to grad⁡(fh)\grad(f^{h}) for a homogenization fhf^{h} of ff.

Outside the class of encompassing polynomials, the following natural question seems absolutely open.

Question 1.3.

Which sequences can be obtained as (dim𝕂Ap⁡(fd))d≥1\bigl(\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f^{d})\bigr)_{d\geq 1}?

Specializing a bit, one could wonder whether knowing first few dimensions is enough to know the whole sequence. This is an open question as well. In subsection 4.2 we answer it for the sequence

d↦(ℓ+d−1d).d\mapsto\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}.

We show that if dim𝕂Ap⁡(fd)\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f^{d}) is maximal for all d≤deg⁡(f)d\leq\deg(f), then ff is encompassing.

1.3. Applications to complexity theory

In the last part of the article our main results are:

  1. (1)

    subsection 5.2: deciding the smoothability of algebras implies estimating border rank of tensors, up to a factor of 1/21/2,

  2. (2)

    subsection 5.2: deciding the smoothability of modules implies estimating border rank of tensors T∈𝕂n⊗𝕂n⊗𝕂nT\in\mathbb{K}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{n} up to an error of nn,

  3. (3)

    introduction of sweet pieces, that is a special class of tensors appearing in complexity theory, see 6.2,

  4. (4)

    estimates of the ranks of sweet pieces of interest in section 6 and section 6.

One of our motivations comes from applications to complexity theory. More precisely, the two major challenges relevant for us are:

  1. (1)

    fast matrix multiplication;

  2. (2)

    special NP-hard problems, like chromatic number of a graph or the set cover problem.

It turns out that in both of the above problems good upper bounds on ranks of Kronecker powers of special tensors can lead to very surprising upper bounds on complexity. Let us explain in detail how smoothable algebras, their tensor powers, and Veronese subalgebras appear in the above problems.

The complexity of matrix multiplication is governed by the constant ω\omega, see [25, 64] for a detailed exposition, or [69]*Chapter 9.3 for a quick introduction to the topic. The state-of-the-art method to bound ω\omega from above is due to D. Coppersmith and S. Winograd (see [35]). The exact value of ω\omega remains unknown, although upper bounds have been improved in recent years, showing that ω<2.38\omega<2.38, see [35, 3, 78, 1]. The core method starts with a smoothable algebra AA, which is apolar to a quadric. The bilinear map given by multiplication in AA gives rise to a tensor TAT_{A}, known as the Coppersmith-Winograd tensor,which is of minimal border rank dim𝕂A\dim_{\mathbb{K}}A, see [19]. One identifies direct sums of matrix multiplication tensors as restriction of the tensor associated to A⊗dA^{\otimes d} for large dd, which is also the dd-th Kronecker power of TAT_{A}. This allows to upper bound the border rank of the direct sums by (dim𝕂A)d(\dim_{\mathbb{K}}A)^{d}. Using Schönhage’s τ\tau-theorem [25]*§15.5 one obtains upper bounds on ω\omega.

The key step in this method is to identify a highly symmetric subtensor S​PdSP_{d} of TA⊗dT_{A^{\otimes d}} and to prove that it restricts to the above direct sum of matrix multiplications. It turns out that S​PdSP_{d} in many cases is not only a restriciton of the tensor associated to A⊗d{A^{\otimes d}}, but also of its much smaller Veronese subalgebra. Thus, obtaining bounds on border rank or smoothable rank of tensors associated to Veronese subalgebras of smoothable algebras would lead to new upper bounds on ω\omega. In particular, if S​PdSP_{d} was of minimal asymptotic rank, then ω=2\omega=2.

For the second point one considers some of the well-known NP-hard problems. Very recent work [18, 72, 17] identifies certain families of tensors for which upper bounds on rank would provide algorithms of unexpectedly low complexity. For example for a family of tensors S​PdSP_{d} one could check, in the randomized setting, whether there exist three sets from a given three (balanced) families whose union is the whole given set of size nn, in time CnC^{n} for some constant C<2C<2.

In our work, we identify the properties of S​PdSP_{d} to define the class of tensors called the sweet pieces, see 6.2. As argued above, upper bounds on the ranks of sweet pieces are of central importance. We provide new methods to upper bound not only border ranks, but also ranks of the sweet pieces S​PdSP_{d}, see Sections 6 and 6 and section 6. We apply these results to obtain new, best upper bounds for rank and border rank of S​PdSP_{d} tensors that appear in the Coppersmith-Winograd tensor and in the work of K. Pratt [72], see below.

Proposition 1.3 (section 6).

Given nonnegative parameters p,qp,q such that 3​p+3​q=13p+3q=1 one considers the sweet piece for the NN-th Kronecker power of the n×n×nn\times n\times n Coppersmith-Winograd tensor C​WnCW_{n}. The rank of any such sweet piece is smaller than

nN−(N(2​p+2​q)​N+1)​(n−1)(p+q)​N−1.n^{N}-\binom{N}{(2p+2q)N+1}(n-1)^{(p+q)N-1}.

In particular, it is smaller than the border rank of (C​Wn)⊠N(CW_{n})^{\boxtimes N}.

Proposition 1.3 (section 6).

Consider the tensors associated to the bilinear multiplication map

(ℂ⁡[x]/(x2)⊗3​k)k×(ℂ⁡[x]/(x2)⊗3​k)k→(ℂ⁡[x]/(x2)⊗3​k)2​k({\mathbb{C}[x]/(x^{2})}^{\otimes 3k})_{k}\times({\mathbb{C}[x]/(x^{2})}^{\otimes 3k})_{k}\rightarrow({\mathbb{C}[x]/(x^{2})}^{\otimes 3k})_{2k}

where the subindex denotes the degree (these are precisely the tensors from [72]). These tensors have rank at most

12​8k−∑i=k+1⌊3​k/2⌋(3​k2​i).\frac{1}{2}8^{k}-\sum_{i=k+1}^{\lfloor 3k/2\rfloor}\binom{3k}{2i}.

The improvements in the upper bounds may not seem large. Indeed, to obtain new estimates for ω\omega, one needs to obtain in subsection 1.3 an upper bound of the form nC​Nn^{CN}, where C<1C<1. Nevertheless, we believe that improving the upper bounds of sweet pieces is important, as e.g. for the set covering problem subexponential improvements may already refute the conjectures about the complexity of the problem [72]*Corollary 1.12. In addition, recently new barrier results appeared [32, 20], which show that it is essentially impossible to prove ω=2\omega=2 using only tensors from a class that includes the Coppersmith-Winograd tensor. However, these barrier results are not valid, if one improves upper bounds on the ranks of the sweet pieces. Experts may notice that the sweet pieces of interest have asymptotically largest subrank.

2. Preliminaries

In the study of tensor decomposition, the quantity that has appeared most frequently in the literature is the Waring rank of a symmetric tensor or, equivalently, of a homogeneous polynomial. For any f∈Sd​Vf\in S^{d}V, the Waring rank, or simply the rank, of ff is the minimal number of linear forms such that ff can be expressed as a linear combination of the dd-th powers of such forms. Over the years, many other concepts related to symmetric tensors have been introduced, such as border rank, cactus rank, and smoothable rank. In general, important tools for tensor decompositions are provided by the theory of apolarity. In this article we work over an algebraically closed field 𝕂\mathbb{K} of characteristic zero.

2.1. Apolarity

Let VV be an arbitrary (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional vector space over 𝕂\mathbb{K}. Let

ℛgl:-S⁡(V),𝒟gl:-S⁡(V∗)\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}\coloneq S(V),\qquad\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}\coloneq S(V^{*})

denote the symmetric algebra of VV and its dual, respectively. Some zero-dimensional projective schemes below will live in in ℙ⁡(V)=Proj⁡S⁡(V∗)=Proj⁡𝒟gl\mathbb{P}(V)=\Proj S(V^{*})=\Proj\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}. Let

(ℛgl)d:-Sd​V,(𝒟gl)d:-Sd​V∗(\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}})_{d}\coloneq S^{d}V,\qquad(\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}})_{d}\coloneq S^{d}V^{*}

denote the dd-th symmetric powers of VV and V∗V^{*}, respectively. The ring 𝒟gl\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}} acts on ℛgl\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}} so that every α∈V∗\alpha\in V^{*} acts as a partial derivative. If we fix the dual bases {x0,…,xn}\{x_{0},\dots,x_{n}\} and {α0,…,αn}\{\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{n}\} of VV and V∗V^{*} respectively, we can identify their symmetric algebras as

ℛgl=𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn],𝒟gl=𝕂⁡[α0,…,αn].\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}=\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\dots,x_{n}],\qquad\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}=\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{n}].

For such fixed bases, we also consider

ℛ=𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn],𝒟=𝕂⁡[α1,…,αn].\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}],\qquad\mathcal{D}=\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n}].

The ring 𝒟\mathcal{D} can be identified with the ring of functions on the affine patch (x0≠0)⊂ℙ⁡(V)(x_{0}\neq 0)\subset\mathbb{P}(V). We denote the monomials in ℛgl\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}} and 𝒟gl\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}} by

𝐱𝐦:-x0m0⋯xnmn,𝜶𝐦:-α0m0⋯αnmn,\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{m}}\coloneq x_{0}^{m_{0}}\cdots x_{n}^{m_{n}},\qquad\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{m}}\coloneq\alpha_{0}^{m_{0}}\cdots\alpha_{n}^{m_{n}},

for any multi-index 𝐦=(m0,…,mn)∈ℕn+1\mathbf{m}=(m_{0},\dots,m_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n+1}. For such an 𝐦\mathbf{m}, we denote 𝐦!:-m0!⋯mn!\mathbf{m}!\coloneq m_{0}!\cdots m_{n}!. The polarization map is defined for monomials 𝜶𝐤∈𝒟gl\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{k}}\in\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}} and 𝐱𝐦∈ℛgl\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{m}}\in\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}} as

𝜶𝐤∘𝐱𝐦:-{𝐦!(𝐦−𝐤)!​𝐱𝐦−𝐤if 𝐦−𝐤≥0,0otherwise.\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{k}}\circ\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{m}}\coloneq\begin{cases}\dfrac{\mathbf{m}!}{(\mathbf{m}-\mathbf{k})!}\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{m}-\mathbf{k}}\quad&\text{if $\mathbf{m}-\mathbf{k}\geq 0$},\\[8.61108pt] 0\quad&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
Definition 2.1.

The apolarity action of 𝒟gl\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}} on ℛgl\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}} is defined by linearly extending the polarization maps for each component of 𝒟gl\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}} and ℛgl\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}. It is denoted by ∘:𝒟gl×ℛgl→ℛgl\circ\colon\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}\times\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}\to\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}, and gives (σ,f)↦σ∘f(\sigma,f)\mapsto\sigma\circ f.

By fixing a polynomial f∈ℛglf\in\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}, it is possible to define a function that describes the apolarity action of the space 𝒟gl\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}} on ff.

Definition 2.2.

For any f∈ℛglf\in\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}, the catalecticant map of ff is defined as the linear map

(2.3)

The annihilator (or apolar ideal) of ff is the kernel of Catf\Cat_{f}, that is, the set

Ann⁡(f):-{σ∈𝒟gl|σ∘f=0}.\Ann(f)\coloneq\Set{\sigma\in\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}}{\sigma\circ f=0}.

The annihilator of a polynomial ff was called principal system by F. S. Macaulay and its quotient

Ap⁡(f):-𝒟glAnn⁡(f)\Ap(f)\coloneq\frac{{\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}}}{\Ann(f)}

is also called the apolar algebra of ff. The apolar algebra was introduced in [67] by F. S. Macaulay, see also [52]*p. XX and [40]*p. 75. The above definition immediately extends to an arbitrary number of polynomials.

Definition 2.4.

Let f1,…,fr∈ℛglf_{1},\dots,f_{r}\in\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}. The annihilator of f1,…,frf_{1},\dots,f_{r} is the ideal

Ann⁡(f1,…,fr):-⋂i=1rAnn⁡(fi).\Ann(f_{1},\dots,f_{r})\coloneq\bigcap_{i=1}^{r}\Ann(f_{i}).

The apolar algebra of f1,…,frf_{1},\dots,f_{r} is the quotient space

Ap⁡(f1,…,fr):-𝒟glAnn⁡(f1,…,fr).\Ap(f_{1},\dots,f_{r})\coloneq\frac{{\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}}}{\Ann(f_{1},\dots,f_{r})}.

In the particular case of a single polynomial f∈ℛglf\in\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}, we have the isomorphism of 𝒟gl\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}-modules

(2.5) 𝒟gl∘f≃Ap⁡(f).\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}\circ f\simeq\Ap(f).

A polynomial f∈ℛglf\in\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}} is concise if it cannot be written, possibly after a change of coordinates, using less than nn variables. Equivalently, the polynomial ff is concise if

Ann⁡(f)∩𝒟gl≤1={0}.\Ann(f)\cap{\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}}_{\leq 1}=\{0\}.

The discussion above can be repeated for the subrings ℛ\mathcal{R}, 𝒟\mathcal{D}: the apolarity action restricts from 𝒟gl\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}}, ℛgl\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}} to 𝒟\mathcal{D}, ℛ\mathcal{R}, for a polynomial f∈ℛf\in\mathcal{R} we obtain its apolar algebra Ap⁡(f)=𝒟/Ann⁡(f)\Ap(f)=\mathcal{D}/\Ann(f) etc.

2.2. Ranks of tensors

In this section we recall several notions of rank that will be useful below. A crucial tool for providing upper bounds for the rank is the classical apolarity lemma.

Lemma 2.5 (Apolarity lemma).

Let F∈(ℛgl)d{F}\in(\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}})_{d}be a homogeneous polynomial and Z⊆ℙnZ\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n} be a finite scheme. Let

νd:ℙ⁡((ℛgl)1)→ℙ⁡((ℛgl)d)\nu_{d}\colon\mathbb{P}\bigl((\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}})_{1}\bigr)\to\mathbb{P}\bigl((\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}})_{d}\bigr)

be the dd-Veronese map. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    [F]∈⟨νd​(Z)⟩[{F}]\in\langle\nu_{d}(Z)\rangle;

  2. (2)

    I⁡(Z)⊆Ann⁡(F)I(Z)\subseteq\Ann({F}).

If they hold, we say that ZZ is apolar to F{F}.

The lemma gives rise to three notions of rank, and also gives an alternative but equivalent definition of Waring rank.

Definition 2.6.

The cactus rank of FF is the minimum degree of a scheme ZZ apolar to FF. The smoothable rank of FF is the minimal degree of such a ZZ, where ZZ is smoothable (see §2.4 below). The Waring rank of FF is the minimum degree of such a ZZ, where ZZ is a tuple of points.

The cactus rank was introduced under the name of scheme length by A. Iarrobino and V. Kanev (see [52]*Definition 5.1). The term cactus rank was first used by K. Ranestad and F.-O. Schreyer in [73], inspired by the notion of cactus variety, introduced by W. Buczyńska and J. Buczyński in [21]. The cactus rank was analyzed in several other papers, such as [5, 11, 4]. The smoothable rank was also first introduced in [73], motivated by several results appearing in [8, 21, 23]. For a homogeneous polynomial F{F}, we denote its smoothable rank by smrk⁡F\smrk{F} and its cactus rank by crk⁡F\crk{F}. For any F{F} we have inequalities

crk⁡F≤smrk⁡F≤rk⁡F,\crk{F}\leq\smrk{F}\leq\rk{F},

which can be strict in general, see, for example, [22, 49].

2.3. Tautological schemes

In general, the construction of apolar schemes for a given form is a subtle problem. There are several papers in the literature that treat these objects, such as [21, 31, 44, 73].

A clear and general procedure is provided by A. Bernardi and K. Ranestad in [11] and later in [9]*section 4. This strategy allows to relate homogeneous polynomials to their dehomogenizations.

Before proceeding further, we warn the reader about one known caveat: Theorem 3 in [11] is incorrect as stated, see corrigendum [12]. A counterexample is subsection 1.2. The source of the problem is the lack of constants in the last line of the proof of [11]*Lemma 2, see (2.7) below. As far as we know, the results of [9]*section 4 are fine. However, [9] uses the contraction action instead of differentiation (see [52]*Appendix A for a comparison of the two actions). The whole problem may seem notational and negligible, but it is unavoidable and led us to the introduction of twists above. subsection 5.1 below shows that they are necessary.

In the current article, we do not introduce the contraction action directly. Rather, we only introduce the necessary notation and refer the reader to [9] and [52]*Appendix A for details.

The main result we use is the following proposition.

Proposition 2.6 ([9]*Corollary 4 or corrected [11]*Lemma 2).

Let F∈ℛgl=𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn]F\in\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}=\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}] be an arbitrary form and let

ZF,x0:=Spec⁡Ap⁡(F|x0=1)⊆(x0≠0)⊆ℙn.Z_{F,x_{0}}:=\Spec\Ap(F|_{x_{0}=1})\subseteq(x_{0}\neq 0)\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n}.

Then the scheme ZF,x0Z_{F,x_{0}} is apolar to tw⁡(F)\mathrm{tw}(F).

Proof.

We follow the notation of [11]*Lemma 2. Let dd be the degree of FF. Take a homogeneous G∈𝒟glG\in\mathcal{D}^{\rm{gl}} such that its dehomogenization g=G|α0=1g=G|_{\alpha_{0}=1} is apolar to f=F|x0=1f=F|_{x_{0}=1}. If the degree of GG is higher than dd, then the apolarity is clear. Otherwise, write

g=gd+⋯+g0,F|x0=1=fd+⋯+f0,g=g_{d}+\cdots+g_{0},\qquad F|_{x_{0}=1}=f_{d}+\cdots+f_{0},

where fif_{i} and gig_{i} are homogeneous of degree ii. The apolarity reduces to

∑jgj∘fj+e=0\sum_{j}g_{j}\circ f_{j+e}=0

for every ee. We compute

(2.7) G∘tw⁡(F)=∑e∑j1(d−(e+j))!​(α0d−j∘x0d−(e+j))​gj∘fe+j=∑e1e!​x0e​∑jgj∘fe+j=0.∎G\circ\mathrm{tw}(F)=\sum_{e}\sum_{j}\frac{1}{(d-(e+j))!}(\alpha_{0}^{d-j}\circ x_{0}^{d-(e+j)})g_{j}\circ f_{e+j}=\sum_{e}\frac{1}{e!}x_{0}^{e}\sum_{j}g_{j}\circ f_{e+j}=0.\qed

2.4. Smoothability

subsection 2.2 and subsection 2.3 are powerful results that can be useful in determining upper bounds. To use them to determine smoothable rank, it is necessary to discuss the notion of smoothability. We recall that the Hilbert scheme Hilbr​(𝔸n)\mathrm{Hilb}_{r}(\mathbb{A}^{n}) of rr points in the affine space 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} is a scheme parameterizing all finite subschemes of 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} of degree rr. It was first introduced by A. Grothendieck in [47] and it is a very important object in algebraic geometry, widely used in the literature (see, e.g., [76, 70, 13] for introductions). Denoting by Hilbr0​(𝔸n)\mathrm{Hilb}_{r}^{0}(\mathbb{A}^{n}) the open subset of Hilbr​(𝔸n)\mathrm{Hilb}_{r}(\mathbb{A}^{n}) consisting of the rr-tuples of distinct points in 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}, we say that a scheme Z⊆𝔸nZ\subseteq\mathbb{A}^{n} is smoothable if it is contained in the closure of Hilbr0​(𝔸n)\mathrm{Hilb}_{r}^{0}(\mathbb{A}^{n}). The smoothability does not depend on the embedding of ZZ, only on ZZ itself. Moreover, a finite scheme ZZ is smoothable if and only if all of its irreducible components are smoothable (see [24]*Theorem 1.1). For more details on smoothability, the reader may consult [52, 24, 28, 54].

Let 𝒟:-𝕂⁡[α1,…,αn]\mathcal{D}\coloneq\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n}] be the coordinate ring of 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}. Our interest focuses on the smoothability of symmetric powers of algebras (see §5.1), and we will see that it is cumbersome to consider them as quotients of 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Thus, it is also important to consider smoothability from the point of view of non-embedded 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebras.

Definition 2.8.

A finite 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra AA is said to be smoothable if there exists a homomorphism 𝕂⁡[[t]]→𝒜\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]\to\mathcal{A}, where 𝕂⁡[[t]]\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!] is the formal power series ring in tt and 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a 𝕂⁡[[t]]\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]-algebra such that the special fiber 𝒜/t​𝒜\mathcal{A}/t\mathcal{A} is isomorphic to AA as an 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra, the generic fiber 𝒜⁡[t−1]\mathcal{A}[t^{-1}] is a smooth 𝕂​[[t]]​[t−1]\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!][t^{-1}]-algebra, and 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a free 𝕂⁡[[t]]\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]-module.

The last two definitions are equivalent thanks to the following result.

Lemma 2.8 ([28]*Lemma 4.1).

Let I⊆𝒟I\subseteq\mathcal{D} be an ideal such that dim𝕂𝒟/I=r\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{D}/I=r. Then Spec⁡(𝒟/I)\Spec(\mathcal{D}/I) is in the smoothable component of Hilbr​(𝔸n)\mathrm{Hilb}_{r}(\mathbb{A}^{n}) if and only if 𝒟/I\mathcal{D}/I is a smoothable 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra in the sense of 2.8.

For any scheme Z=Spec⁡(𝒟/I)⊆𝔸nZ=\Spec(\mathcal{D}/I)\subseteq\mathbb{A}^{n}, much is known about smoothability of ZZ for small values of deg⁡(Z)=dim𝕂𝒟/I\deg(Z)=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{D}/I. Indeed, all schemes ZZ such that deg⁡(Z)≤7\deg(Z)\leq 7 are smoothable ([28]) and all Gorenstein schemes ZZ such that deg⁡(Z)≤13\deg(Z)\leq 13 are smoothable ([29]). However, when deg⁡(Z)\deg(Z) is larger the situation is much more complicated. The known classes of smoothable ZZ are:

  1. (1)

    Z⊆𝔸2Z\subseteq\mathbb{A}^{2}

  2. (2)

    Z⊆𝔸3Z\subseteq\mathbb{A}^{3} Gorenstein;

  3. (3)

    ZZ given by a locally complete intersection or, more generally, linked to a smoothable scheme;

  4. (4)

    ZZ given by a monomial ideal in an 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}.

Disjoint union and product of smoothable schemes are smoothable. While there are many other constructions that give specific examples of smoothable schemes, it seems that the above are the only general ones known. In §5.2 we show that being able to decide whether explicit, simple algebras are smoothable or not, would provide upper and lower bounds on tensor border rank that are much better than state-of-the-art techniques.

2.5. Secant varieties and border rank

When dealing with decompositions of homogeneous polynomials, there is another quantity to consider, namely the border rank of a form. The notion of border rank of an arbitrary tensor was first introduced in 1979 by D. Bini, M. Capovani, G. Lotti, and F. Romani in [15], and then named that way in the following year by D. Bini, G. Lotti, and F. Romani in [16], where the authors defined it as the minimum number of decomposable tensors required to approximate a tensor with an arbitrarily small error. The analog for homogeneous polynomials is defined in the same way. For a homogeneous polynomial F{F}, the border rank of F{F}, denoted by brk⁡F\brk{F}, is the smallest natural number rr such that F{F} is in the closure of a set of polynomials that have rank ≤r\leq r. The closure is taken in the Zariski topology. For 𝕂=ℂ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C} the closure coincides with the closure in the Euclidean topology.

Determining the border rank of a given homogeneous polynomial is in general a very difficult problem. However, again, much information is known for small values of nn and dd (see, e.g., [65, 33, 46, 62, 42, 45]). A typical example illustrating the difference between rank and border rank is given by a monomial of the type x1d−1​x2x_{1}^{d-1}x_{2}, for any d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}. In fact, its rank is equal to dd, but its border rank is 22, as we can express it as

x1d−1​x2=1d⋅limt→01t​((x1+t​x2)d−x1d).x_{1}^{d-1}x_{2}=\frac{1}{d}\cdot\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t}\bigl((x_{1}+tx_{2})^{d}-x_{1}^{d}\bigr).

The catalecticant rank is a known lower bound for the border rank of a form F∈ℛdgl{F}\in\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}}_{d}, historically attributed to J. J. Sylvester see [77].It states that for every k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} we have

(2.9) brk⁡F≥rk⁡(CatF)k,\brk{F}\geq\rk(\Cat_{{F}})_{k},

where (CatF)k(\Cat_{{F}})_{k} is the kk-th catalecticant matrix, see (2.3).

The catalecticant lower bound, usually taken for k≃d/2k\simeq d/2, is very powerful when dd is large with respect to rr. For example, it gives set-theoretic equations of the rr-th secant variety σr​(νd​(ℙn))\sigma_{r}\bigl(\nu_{d}(\mathbb{P}^{n})\bigr) when d≥2​rd\geq 2r and r≤13r\leq 13, see [21]*Theorem 1.1 and §8.1. When rr is large with respect to dd, the bound is very weak and there are few explicit classes of ff for which equality holds: mostly additive decompositions, such as

F≔x1d+…+xnd,{F}\coloneqq x_{1}^{d}+\ldots+x_{n}^{d},

and more generally forms in disjoint sets of variables, such as tangential generalized additive decompositions of the type

F≔x1d−1​x2+x3d−1​x4+…+x2​n−1d−1​x2​n,{F}\coloneqq x_{1}^{d-1}x_{2}+x_{3}^{d-1}x_{4}+\ldots+x_{2n-1}^{d-1}x_{2n},

or yet more generally the GADs, see, e.g., [10]. All the examples known to the authors have maxi⁡rk⁡(CatF)i\max_{i}\rk(\Cat_{{F}})_{i} equal to nn or slightly higher.

There are several examples in the literature concerning the analysis of the rank of the catalecticant matrices of certain homogeneous polynomials (see [6]*Example 2.21 for the case of monomials, see also [52]*p. 198). A special case concerns the powers of quadratic forms. Given any quadratic form qnq_{n} of rank equal to nn, B. Reznick proves that for every integer d≥1d\geq 1 the catalecticant matrices of qndq_{n}^{d} are all of full rank.

Theorem 2.9 ([74]*Theorem 8.15 using [74]*Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 3.16, see also [46]*Theorem 2.2, [42]*Proposition 3.2).

For a quadratic form qn∈(ℛgl)2q_{n}\in(\mathcal{R}^{\rm{gl}})_{2} of rank nn and for any d≥1d\geq 1 we have

brk⁡(qnd)≥(n+d−1d).\brk(q_{n}^{d})\geq\binom{n+d-1}{d}.

A notable fact is that the border rank and the smoothable rank can be compared. Indeed, as observed by A. Bernardi, J. Brachat, and B. Mourrain in [6]*Remark 2.7, using [52]*Lemma 5.17, we have

(2.10) brk⁡F≤smrk⁡F.\brk{F}\leq\smrk{F}.

There are cases where the equality in formula (2.10) does not hold. Several examples of polynomials with border rank strictly lower than the smoothable rank are given by W. Buczyńska and J. Buczyński in [22].

2.6. Lowest and top degree forms

Some of the proofs below make use of the theory of top and lowest degree forms, which we briefly review here (see [53]*§1 for details). Write a polynomial f∈ℛf\in\mathcal{R} as

f=fe+fe+1+…+fd,f=f_{e}+f_{e+1}+\ldots+f_{d},

for some e∈ℕe\in\mathbb{N}, where fi∈ℛf_{i}\in\mathcal{R} is homogeneous of degree ii for e≤i≤de\leq i\leq d and fe,fd≠0f_{e},f_{d}\neq 0. Then the lowest degree form and the top degree form of ff are respectively the homogeneous polynomials

ldf⁡(f):-fe,tdf⁡(f):-fd.\ldf(f)\coloneq f_{e},\qquad\tdf(f)\coloneq f_{d}.

In general none of these is a monomial. Analogous definitions can be made for any polynomial σ∈𝒟\sigma\in\mathcal{D}.

For a 𝒟\mathcal{D}-submodule M⊆ℛM\subseteq\mathcal{R}, we define the space of the lowest degree forms and the space of the top degree forms as the 𝕂\mathbb{K}-linear spaces given by

ldf⁡(M):-⟨{ldf⁡(f)|f∈M}⟩,tdf⁡(M):-⟨{tdf⁡(f)|f∈M}⟩,\ldf(M)\coloneq\langle\Set{\ldf(f)}{f\in M}\rangle,\qquad\tdf(M)\coloneq\langle\Set{\tdf(f)}{f\in M}\rangle,

respectively. Then ldf⁡(M)\ldf(M) and tdf⁡(M)\tdf(M) are also 𝒟\mathcal{D}-submodules. In particular, for any ideal I⊆𝒟I\subseteq\mathcal{D} such that 𝒟≥r⊆I\mathcal{D}_{\geq r}\subseteq I for r≫0r{\gg 0}, we can define tdf⁡(I)\tdf(I), which is the 𝕂\mathbb{K}-linear space spanned by the set

{tdf⁡(σ)|σ∈I}.\Set{\tdf(\sigma)}{\sigma\in I}.

It is an ideal.

Lemma 2.10.

Let MM be a finitely generated 𝒟\mathcal{D}-submodule of ℛ\mathcal{R} and let I=Ann⁡(M)I=\Ann(M). Then

Ann⁡(ldf⁡(M))=tdf⁡(I).\Ann\bigl(\ldf(M)\bigr)=\tdf(I).
Proof.

The subspace ldf⁡(M)\ldf(M) is a 𝒟\mathcal{D}-submodule of ℛ\mathcal{R}. Since II annihilates MM, also tdf⁡(I)\tdf(I) annihilates ldf⁡(M)\ldf(M). Therefore, we must have the inclusion

tdf⁡(I)⊆Ann⁡(ldf⁡(M)).\tdf(I)\subseteq\Ann\bigl(\ldf(M)\bigr).

The spaces MM and 𝒟/Ann⁡(M)\mathcal{D}/\Ann(M) are dual, so they have the same dimension. We obtain

dim𝕂(𝒟/Ann⁡(ldf⁡(M)))=dim𝕂ldf⁡(M)=dim𝕂M=dim𝕂(𝒟/I)=dim𝕂(𝒟/tdf⁡(I))=d,\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Bigl(\mathcal{D}/\Ann\bigl(\ldf(M)\bigr)\Bigr)=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\ldf(M)=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}M=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}(\mathcal{D}/I)=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\mathcal{D}/\tdf(I)\bigr)=d,

so tdf⁡(I)\tdf(I) and Ann⁡(ldf⁡(M))\Ann\bigl(\ldf(M)\bigr) have the same (finite!) codimension, and so the inclusion is an equality. ∎

2.7. Iarrobino’s symmetric decomposition

In the following, in §4.2 we will need a bit of theory of nonhomogeneous Gorenstein algebras, as developed by Iarrobino [53]*chapter 2.

Let ff be a polynomial and A:-Ap⁡(f)A\coloneq\Ap(f). We have

𝒟>deg⁡(f)⊆Ann⁡(f),\mathcal{D}_{>\deg(f)}\subseteq\Ann(f),

so AA is a local ring with the maximal ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m} being the image of (𝒟)≥1(\mathcal{D})_{\geq 1}. We have a bilinear map μ:A×A→𝕂\mu\colon A\times A\to\mathbb{K} given by

μ⁡(a1,a2):-((a1​a2)∘f)0,\mu(a_{1},a_{2})\coloneq\bigl((a_{1}a_{2})\circ f\bigr)_{0},

where (−)0(-)_{0} denotes the constant part of a polynomial and the action ∘\circ is the apolarity action given in 2.1. The whole operation is well defined because Ann⁡(f)\Ann(f) by definition annihilates ff, so (−)∘f(-)\circ f descends to Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f). For every 𝕂\mathbb{K}-subspace L⊆AL\subseteq A we define

L⟂:-{a∈A|μ⁡(a,L)=0}.L^{\perp}\coloneq\Set{a\in A}{\mu(a,L)=0}.

We have the following properties:

  1. (1)

    the pairing μ\mu is perfect;

  2. (2)

    for any mm we have (𝔪m)⟂=(0:𝔪m)(\mathfrak{m}^{m})^{\perp}=(0:\mathfrak{m}^{m});

  3. (3)

    for any mm the pairing μ\mu induces a perfect pairing

    (2.11)

The following lemma is all we will use in the sequel. It is very simple in the case of homogeneous polynomials, but subtler in the nonhomogeneous case.

Lemma 2.11.

Let f∈ℛf\in\mathcal{R} be a polynomial, let m≥0m\geq 0 be fixed and let σ1,…,σl∈𝒟≥m+Ann⁡(f)\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{l}\in\mathcal{D}_{\geq m}+\Ann(f) be elements such that no nonzero 𝕂\mathbb{K}-linear combination of σ1,…,σl\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{l} lies in 𝒟≥m+1+Ann⁡(f)\mathcal{D}_{\geq m+1}+\Ann(f). Then there exist τ1,…,τl∈𝒟\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{l}\in\mathcal{D} such that the following conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    deg⁡(τj∘f)≤m\deg(\tau_{j}\circ f)\leq m for every jj;

  2. (2)

    (τj​σj)∘f=1(\tau_{j}\sigma_{j})\circ f=1 for every jj and (τi​σj)∘f=0(\tau_{i}\sigma_{j})\circ f=0 for every i≠ji\neq j.

Proof.

The surjection 𝒟→Ap⁡(f)\mathcal{D}\to\Ap(f) sends 𝒟≥m\mathcal{D}_{\geq m} onto 𝔪m\mathfrak{m}^{m}. Consider the classes σ¯1,…,σ¯l\overline{\sigma}_{1},\ldots,\overline{\sigma}_{l} in 𝔪m\mathfrak{m}^{m}. By assumption, they yield nonzero and linearly independent elements of 𝔪m/𝔪m+1\mathfrak{m}^{m}/\mathfrak{m}^{m+1}. Complete them to a basis of 𝔪m/𝔪m+1\mathfrak{m}^{m}/\mathfrak{m}^{m+1} and let τ¯1,…,τ¯l∈(0:𝔪m+1)\overline{\tau}_{1},\ldots,\overline{\tau}_{l}\in(0:\mathfrak{m}^{m+1}) be the duals of σ¯1,…,σ¯l\overline{\sigma}_{1},\ldots,\overline{\sigma}_{l} under the perfect pairing of formula (2.11). Let τ1,…,τl∈𝒟\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{l}\in\mathcal{D} be any lifts of τ¯1,…,τ¯l\overline{\tau}_{1},\ldots,\overline{\tau}_{l}. For every jj we have 𝔪m+1​τ¯j=0\mathfrak{m}^{m+1}\overline{\tau}_{j}=0, so 𝒟≥m+1​(τj∘f)=0\mathcal{D}_{\geq m+1}(\tau_{j}\circ f)=0. Hence, deg⁡(τj∘f)≤m\deg(\tau_{j}\circ f)\leq m, which proves (1).

By construction of μ¯\overline{\mu}, the constant μ¯​(σ¯i,τ¯j)\overline{\mu}(\overline{\sigma}_{i},\overline{\tau}_{j}) is the degree zero part of (σi​τj)∘f(\sigma_{i}\tau_{j})\circ f. By the choice of τ¯j\overline{\tau}_{j}, we have

σ¯i​τ¯j∈𝔪m⋅(0:𝔪m+1)⊆(0:𝔪),\overline{\sigma}_{i}\overline{\tau}_{j}\in\mathfrak{m}^{m}\cdot(0:\mathfrak{m}^{m+1})\subseteq(0:\mathfrak{m}),

so σ¯i​τ¯j​𝔪=0\overline{\sigma}_{i}\overline{\tau}_{j}\mathfrak{m}=0 and hence 𝒟≥1∘(σi​τj∘f)=0\mathcal{D}_{\geq 1}\circ(\sigma_{i}\tau_{j}\circ f)=0. It follows that σi​τj∘f∈𝕂\sigma_{i}\tau_{j}\circ f\in\mathbb{K} is a constant polynomial. We can then identify it with the constant μ¯​(σ¯i,τ¯j)\overline{\mu}(\overline{\sigma}_{i},\overline{\tau}_{j}) and obtain part (2). ∎

3. Apolar algebras of powers of polynomials

In this section we focus on the apolar algebras of the powers of of a given polynomial ff. It turns out that it is easier to start with the tensor powers.

For a number d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} take the dd-th tensor power ℛ⊠d\mathcal{R}^{\boxtimes d} and its dual space 𝒟⊠d\mathcal{D}^{\boxtimes d}. These can be identified as the polynomial rings

ℛ⊠d:-𝕂[xi​j|i=1,…,n,j=1,…,d],𝒟⊠d:-𝕂[αi​j|i=1,…,n,j=1,…,d],\mathcal{R}^{\boxtimes d}\coloneq\mathbb{K}[x_{ij}\ |\ i=1,\dots,n,\,j=1,\dots,d],\qquad\mathcal{D}^{\boxtimes d}\coloneq\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{ij}\ |\ i=1,\dots,n,\,j=1,\dots,d],

respectively. For a polynomial f∈ℛf\in\mathcal{R}, its dd-th tensor power f⊠df^{\boxtimes d} is defined as

f⊠d:=f(x11,…,xn​1)f(x12,…,xn​2)⋯f(x1​d,…,xn​d).f^{\boxtimes d}:=f(x_{11},\ldots,x_{n1})f(x_{12},\ldots,x_{n2})\cdots f\left(x_{1d},\ldots,x_{nd}\right).

In the following we will use the notation 𝐱∙j\mathbf{x}_{\bullet j} for x1​j,…,xn​jx_{1j},\ldots,x_{nj} and α∙j\alpha_{\bullet j} for α1​j,…,αn​j\alpha_{1j},\ldots,\alpha_{nj}, where j∈{1,…,d}j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}.

Proposition 3.0 (apolar algebra of the tensor power).

The apolar algebra Ap⁡(f⊠d)\Ap(f^{\boxtimes d}) is isomorphic to Ap⁡(f)⊗d\Ap(f)^{\otimes d}. In particular, it has dimension (dim𝕂Ap⁡(f))d\bigl(\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f)\bigr)^{d}.

Proof.

Let I=Ann⁡(f)I=\Ann(f) and for every j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d, let Ij⊆𝕂⁡[α∙j]I_{j}\subseteq\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{\bullet j}] be a copy of II. Then every IjI_{j} annihilates f⊠df^{\boxtimes d}, so

Ap⁡(f⊠d):-𝒟⊠d/Ann⁡(f⊠d)\Ap(f^{\boxtimes d})\coloneq\mathcal{D}^{\boxtimes d}/\Ann(f^{\boxtimes d})

is a quotient of

𝒟⊠d(I1)+(I2)+⋯+(Id)≃𝕂⁡[α∙1]I1⊗𝕂𝕂⁡[α∙2]I2⊗𝕂⋯⊗𝕂𝕂⁡[α∙d]Id≃Ap(f)⊗⋯⊗Ap(f)=Ap(f)⊗d.\frac{\mathcal{D}^{\boxtimes d}}{(I_{1})+(I_{2})+\cdots+(I_{d})}\simeq\frac{\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{\bullet 1}]}{I_{1}}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}\frac{\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{\bullet 2}]}{I_{2}}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}\cdots\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}\frac{\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{\bullet d}]}{I_{d}}\simeq\Ap(f)\otimes\cdots\otimes\Ap(f)=\Ap(f)^{\otimes d}.

Moreover, if g1,…,gd∈𝒟∘fg_{1},\ldots,g_{d}\in\mathcal{D}\circ f are arbitrary partials of ff, say gi=σi∘fg_{i}=\sigma_{i}\circ f, then

g1(𝐱∙1)⋯gd(𝐱∙d)=(σ1(α∙1)⋯σd(α∙d))∘f⊠d.g_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{\bullet 1})\cdots g_{d}(\mathbf{x}_{\bullet d})=\bigl(\sigma_{1}(\alpha_{\bullet 1})\cdots\sigma_{d}(\alpha_{\bullet d})\bigr)\circ f^{\boxtimes d}.

This shows that the linear space 𝒟⊠d∘f⊠d\mathcal{D}^{\boxtimes d}\circ f^{\boxtimes d} has dimension at least (dim𝕂Ap⁡(f))d\bigl(\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f)\bigr)^{d}. Therefore, by formula (2.5), we also have

dim𝕂(Ap⁡(f⊠d))≤(dim𝕂Ap⁡(f))d.∎\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f^{\boxtimes d})\bigr)\leq\bigl(\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f)\bigr)^{d}.\qed

section 3implies that the algebra Ap⁡(f⊠d)\Ap(f^{\boxtimes d}) is closely related to Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f). For example, if Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) is smoothable by a family 𝕂⁡[[t]]→𝒜\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]\to\mathcal{A}, then Ap⁡(f⊠d)\Ap(f^{\boxtimes d}) is smoothable by a family 𝕂⁡[[t]]→𝒜⊗d\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]\to\mathcal{A}^{\otimes d}.

We now move on to discussing the usual powers fdf^{d}. We will see that the situation here is much more subtle. This might be unexpected, so we give an example. Namely, the dimension of the 𝕂\mathbb{K}-vector space Ap⁡(f2)\Ap(f^{2}) is by no means determined by dim𝕂(Ap⁡(f))\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f)\bigr). In fact it is not determined by the isomorphism class of the algebra Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) itself!

Example 3.0.

Let f:-x12f\coloneq x_{1}^{2} and g:-x12+x2g\coloneq x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}. We have

Ap⁡(f)≃𝕂⁡[ε]/(ε3)≃Ap⁡(g).\Ap(f)\simeq\mathbb{K}[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{3})\simeq\Ap(g).

However, dim𝕂(Ap⁡(f2))=5\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f^{2})\bigr)=5, while dim𝕂(Ap⁡(g2))=6\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(g^{2})\bigr)=6.

We now give a bound on the dimension of Ap⁡(fd)\Ap(f^{d}). It is most convenient to work with the space 𝒟∘fd\mathcal{D}\circ f^{d}. Let ℱ≔𝒟∘f\mathcal{F}\coloneqq\mathcal{D}\circ f. Consider the space

ℱd≔ℱ⋯ℱ⏟d⊆ℛ,\mathcal{F}^{d}\coloneqq\underbrace{\mathcal{F}\cdots\mathcal{F}}_{d}\subseteq\mathcal{R},

where the product is taken dd times. This space contains

fd=f⋯f⏟df^{d}=\underbrace{f\cdots f}_{d}

and it is closed under the action of 𝒟\mathcal{D}, hence

(3.1) 𝒟∘fd⊆ℱd.\mathcal{D}\circ f^{d}\subseteq\mathcal{F}^{d}.

There is also a natural surjective map Sd​ℱ→ℱdS^{d}\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{F}^{d} which maps a formal product of dd elements of ℱ\mathcal{F} to the actual product. All in all we get a diagram

(3.2)
Proposition 3.2 (dimension of the apolar to the symmetric power).

For any arbitrary polynomial ff, let ℓ=dim𝕂(Ap⁡(f))\ell=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f)\bigr). Then we have

dim𝕂(Ap⁡(fd))≤(ℓ+d−1d)\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f^{d})\bigr)\leq\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}

and equality holds if and only if both arrows in diagram (3.2) are bijections.

Proof.

Diagram (3.2) yields inequalities

dim𝕂(Ap⁡(fd))≤dim𝕂ℱd≤dim𝕂Sd​ℱ=(ℓ+d−1d).∎\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f^{d})\bigr)\leq\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{F}^{d}\leq\dim_{\mathbb{K}}S^{d}\mathcal{F}=\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}.\qed

The most interesting case for us is when the dimension of Ap⁡(fd)\Ap(f^{d}) is maximal for all dd. In this case, we say that ff has maximal growth of powers. For this class of polynomials, we show that the problem of section 3 disappears, since the dimension of Ap⁡(fd)\Ap(f^{d}) is determined by dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f), see section 3. For this, we need to switch from spaces of partials to quotients of 𝒟\mathcal{D} and we prepare for this below.

There is a canonical injective homomorphism ιℛ:ℛ↪ℛ⊠d\iota_{\mathcal{R}}\colon\mathcal{R}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{R}^{\boxtimes d} of algebras defined on variables by

ιℛ​(xi):-1d​∑j=1dxi​j.\iota_{\mathcal{R}}\left(x_{i}\right)\coloneq\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_{ij}.

There is a corresponding projection homomorphism πℛ:ℛ⊠d→ℛ\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\colon\mathcal{R}^{\boxtimes d}\to\mathcal{R}, which satisfies the equality πℛ∘ιℛ=idℛ\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\circ\iota_{\mathcal{R}}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{R}} and it is defined by πℛ​(xi​j):-xi\pi_{\mathcal{R}}(x_{ij})\coloneq x_{i} for every i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. We do the same for the space 𝒟⊠d\mathcal{D}^{\boxtimes d}.

To preserve duality, we define the maps ι𝒟:𝒟→𝒟⊠d\iota_{\mathcal{D}}\colon\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}^{\boxtimes d} and π𝒟:𝒟⊠d→𝒟\pi_{\mathcal{D}}\colon\mathcal{D}^{\boxtimes d}\to\mathcal{D} such that

ι𝒟​(αi):-∑j=1dαi​j,π𝒟​(αi​j):-1d​αi,\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\alpha_{i})\coloneq\sum_{j=1}^{d}\alpha_{ij},\qquad\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(\alpha_{ij})\coloneq\frac{1}{d}\alpha_{i},

for every i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n and j=1,…,dj=1,\dots,d. Again, we have π𝒟∘ι𝒟=id𝒟\pi_{\mathcal{D}}\circ\iota_{\mathcal{D}}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{D}}. The duality alluded to above follows from the equality

ι𝒟​(αi)∘ιℛ​(xk)=(∑j=1dαi​j)∘(1d​∑j=1dxk​j)=1d​∑j=1d(αi​j∘xk​j)={1,if i=k,0,otherwise.\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\alpha_{i})\circ\iota_{\mathcal{R}}(x_{k})=\biggl(\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{d}\alpha_{ij}\biggr)\circ\biggl(\dfrac{1}{d}\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_{kj}\biggr)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}(\alpha_{ij}\circ x_{kj})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if $i=k$},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The most important formal property of the above maps is captured by the following statement. The reader will probably recognize that the argument is about the representations of the symmetric group Σd\Sigma_{d}, but we keep the proof elementary.

Lemma 3.2.

Let fj∈𝕂⁡[x∙j]f_{j}\in\mathbb{K}[x_{\bullet j}] for every j=1,…,dj=1,\dots,d. For any σ∈𝒟\sigma\in\mathcal{D} we have

πℛ(ι𝒟(σ)∘(f1⋯fd))=σ∘πℛ(f1⋯fd).\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\bigl(\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\sigma)\circ(f_{1}\cdots f_{d})\bigr)=\sigma\circ\pi_{\mathcal{R}}(f_{1}\cdots f_{d}).
