ι𝒟​(σ)=(α11+α12)​(α21+α22),\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\sigma)=(\alpha_{11}+\alpha_{12})(\alpha_{21}+\alpha_{22}),

hence

ι𝒟​(σ)∘f1​f2=(α11​α21∘f1)​f2+f1​(α12​α22∘f2)+(α11∘f1)​(α22∘f2)+(α21∘f1)​(α12∘f2).\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\sigma)\circ f_{1}f_{2}=(\alpha_{11}\alpha_{21}\circ f_{1})f_{2}+f_{1}(\alpha_{12}\alpha_{22}\circ f_{2})+(\alpha_{11}\circ f_{1})(\alpha_{22}\circ f_{2})+(\alpha_{21}\circ f_{1})(\alpha_{12}\circ f_{2}).

Let f¯i=πℛ​(fi)\overline{f}_{i}=\pi_{\mathcal{R}}(f_{i}). Applying πℛ\pi_{\mathcal{R}} to the right side, we obtain

(α1​α2∘f¯1)​f¯2+f¯1​(α1​α2∘f¯2)+(α1∘f¯1)​(α2∘f¯2)+(α2∘f¯1)​(α1∘f¯2)=(α1​α2)∘(f¯1​f¯2).\bigl(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\circ\overline{f}_{1}\bigr)\overline{f}_{2}+\overline{f}_{1}\bigl(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\circ\overline{f}_{2}\bigr)+\bigl(\alpha_{1}\circ\overline{f}_{1}\bigr)\bigl(\alpha_{2}\circ\overline{f}_{2}\bigr)+\bigl(\alpha_{2}\circ\overline{f}_{1}\bigr)\bigl(\alpha_{1}\circ\overline{f}_{2}\bigr)=(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})\circ\bigl(\overline{f}_{1}\overline{f}_{2}\bigr).
Proof of section 3.

Considering the diagram

we have to prove that it commutes for every σ∈𝒟\sigma\in\mathcal{D} and every f1,…,fdf_{1},\dots,f_{d} with fj∈𝕂⁡[x∙j]f_{j}\in\mathbb{K}[x_{\bullet j}]. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the linear space spanned by all products f1,…,fdf_{1},\ldots,f_{d} as above. Then 𝒫⊆ℛ⊠d\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{R}^{\boxtimes d} is a 𝒟⊠d\mathcal{D}^{\boxtimes d}-submodule, in particular it is a 𝒟\mathcal{D}-submodule. We will prove that for every p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P} and σ∈𝒟\sigma\in\mathcal{D} we have

(3.3) πℛ​(ι𝒟​(σ)∘p)=σ∘πℛ​(p).\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\left(\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\sigma)\circ p\right)=\sigma\circ\pi_{\mathcal{R}}(p).

First, we do it for σ=αi\sigma=\alpha_{i} being a linear form. It is sufficient to check it in the case where pp is a product f1⋯fdf_{1}\cdots f_{d} as above.

πℛ(ι𝒟(αi)∘(f1⋯fd))\displaystyle\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\bigl(\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\alpha_{i})\circ(f_{1}\cdots f_{d})\bigr) =πℛ((αi​1+⋯+αi​d)∘(f1(x∙1)⋯fd(x∙d)))\displaystyle=\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\Bigl((\alpha_{i1}+\cdots+\alpha_{id})\circ\bigl(f_{1}(x_{\bullet 1})\cdots f_{d}(x_{\bullet d})\bigr)\Bigr)
=∑j=1dπℛ(αi​j∘(f1(x∙1)⋯fd(x∙d)))\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\Bigl(\alpha_{ij}\circ\bigl(f_{1}(x_{\bullet 1})\cdots f_{d}(x_{\bullet d})\bigr)\Bigr)
=∑j=1dπℛ​((αi​j∘fj​(x∙j))​∏k≠jfk​(x∙k))\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\biggl(\bigl(\alpha_{ij}\circ f_{j}(x_{\bullet j})\bigr)\prod_{k\neq j}f_{k}(x_{\bullet k})\biggr)
=∑j=1d(αi∘fj​(x∙))​∏k≠jfk​(x∙)\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\bigl(\alpha_{i}\circ f_{j}(x_{\bullet})\bigr)\prod_{k\neq j}f_{k}(x_{\bullet})
(3.4) =αi∘(f1(x∙)⋯fd(x∙))=αi∘πℛ(f1⋯fd).\displaystyle=\alpha_{i}\circ\bigl(f_{1}(x_{\bullet})\cdots f_{d}(x_{\bullet})\bigr)=\alpha_{i}\circ\pi_{\mathcal{R}}(f_{1}\cdots f_{d}).

This proves (3.3) in the case where σ\sigma is a variable. We will now prove (3.3) in the case where σ\sigma is a monomial. We do this by induction on the degree. To do the induction step, suppose that τ=αi​σ\tau=\alpha_{i}\sigma and that (3.3) holds for σ\sigma. Take any p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P}. We have ι𝒟​(σ)∘p∈𝒫\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\sigma)\circ p\in\mathcal{P}, and hence

τ∘πℛ​(p)\displaystyle\tau\circ\pi_{\mathcal{R}}(p) =αi∘(σ∘πℛ​(p))=(3.3)​for​σαi∘(πℛ​(ι𝒟​(σ)∘p))\displaystyle=\alpha_{i}\circ\bigl(\sigma\circ\pi_{\mathcal{R}}(p)\bigr)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eqref{eq:compatibility}\,\mathrm{for}\,\sigma}}{{=}}\alpha_{i}\circ\Bigl(\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\bigl(\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\sigma)\circ p\bigr)\Bigr)
=(3.3)​for​αiπℛ​(ι𝒟​(αi)∘(ι𝒟​(σ)∘p))=πℛ​(ι𝒟​(τ)∘p).\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eqref{eq:compatibility}\,\mathrm{for}\,\alpha_{i}}}{{=}}\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\Bigl(\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\alpha_{i})\circ\bigl(\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\sigma)\circ p\bigr)\Bigr)=\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\bigl(\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\tau)\circ p\bigr).

This concludes the proof of (3.3) for σ\sigma a monomial. For general σ\sigma, the proof follows by linearity. ∎

section 3implies the following key corollary.

Corollary 3.4.

Let f∈ℛf\in\mathcal{R} and d≥1d\geq 1. Take ℓ=dim𝕂(Ap⁡(f))\ell=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f)\bigr). Suppose that

dim𝕂(Ap⁡(fd))=(ℓ+d−1d).\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f^{d})\bigr)=\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}.

Then Ap⁡(fd)\Ap(f^{d}) is isomorphic to Sd​Ap⁡(f)S^{d}\Ap(f).

Proof.

Let σ∈𝒟\sigma\in\mathcal{D}. Then

πℛ​(ι𝒟​(σ)∘f⊠d)=σ∘fd.\pi_{\mathcal{R}}\bigl(\iota_{\mathcal{D}}(\sigma)\circ f^{\boxtimes d}\bigr)=\sigma\circ f^{d}.

In particular, we have

𝒟∩Ann⁡(f⊠d)⊆Ann⁡(fd).\mathcal{D}\cap\Ann(f^{\boxtimes d})\subseteq\Ann(f^{d}).

By the construction of ι𝒟\iota_{\mathcal{D}}, the image of the map

𝒟→𝒟⊠d→Ap⁡(f⊠d)\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}^{\boxtimes d}\to\Ap(f^{\boxtimes d})

lands in the Σd\Sigma_{d}-fixed part, so we obtain the following diagram

(3.5)

By section 3 the algebra Ap⁡(f⊠d)\Ap(f^{\boxtimes d}) is isomorphic to Ap⁡(f)⊗d\Ap(f)^{\otimes d}. The Σd\Sigma_{d}-action on Ap⁡(f⊠d)\Ap(f^{\boxtimes d}) corresponds to permuting factors in Ap⁡(f)⊗d\Ap(f)^{\otimes d}, so that

Ap⁡(f⊠d)Σd≃Sd​(Ap⁡(f))\Ap(f^{\boxtimes d})^{\Sigma_{d}}\simeq S^{d}\bigl(\Ap(f)\bigr)

as algebras. We have

dim𝕂Sd​(Ap⁡(f))=(ℓ+d−1d).\dim_{\mathbb{K}}S^{d}\bigl(\Ap(f)\bigr)=\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}.

By assumption, this is also the dimension of Ap⁡(fd)\Ap(f^{d}). Therefore, both arrows in diagram (3.5) are isomorphisms. The claim follows. ∎

4. Encompassing polynomials

The inequality in section 3 and the consequence of equality in section 3 naturally lead to the question: for which polynomials the equality holds? In this section we answer this question by proving subsection 1.2. The key property for us is given by the following definition.

Definition 4.1.

A polynomial f∈ℛf\in\mathcal{R} is encompassing if there is no nonzero element g∈𝒟∘fg\in\mathcal{D}\circ f such that g≤1=0g_{\leq 1}=0. Equivalently, for any basis {g1,…,gℓ}\{g_{1},\ldots,g_{\ell}\} of 𝒟∘f\mathcal{D}\circ f, the degree ≤1\leq 1 parts (g1)≤1(g_{1})_{\leq 1}, …, (gℓ)≤1(g_{\ell})_{\leq 1} are linearly independent.

We observe how this notion translates to the apolar side.

Lemma 4.1.

A polynomial ff is encompassing if and only if the image of 𝒟≤1\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1} in Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) spans this algebra (as a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-vector space).

Proof.

Let I:-Ann⁡(f)I\coloneq\Ann(f) and let ℓ:=dim𝕂(Ap⁡(f))\ell:=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\Ap(f)\bigr). The dimension of the image im⁡(𝒟≤1)⊆Ap⁡(f)\im(\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1})\subseteq\Ap(f) is

1+n−dim𝕂(I∩𝒟≤1).1+n-\dim_{\mathbb{K}}(I\cap\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1}).

A polynomial is linear if and only if its top degree form is linear, hence

1+n−dim𝕂(I∩𝒟≤1)=1+n−dim𝕂(tdf⁡(I))≤1.1+n-\dim_{\mathbb{K}}(I\cap\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1})=1+n-\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\tdf(I)\bigr)_{\leq 1}.

By subsection 2.6 we have

1+n−dim𝕂(tdf⁡(I))≤1=dim𝕂(ldf⁡(𝒟∘f))≤1.1+n-\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\tdf(I)\bigr)_{\leq 1}=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\ldf(\mathcal{D}\circ f)\bigr)_{\leq 1}.

The polynomial ff is encompassing if and only if

dim𝕂(ldf⁡(𝒟∘f))≤1=ℓ.\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\bigl(\ldf(\mathcal{D}\circ f)\bigr)_{\leq 1}=\ell.

This is true if and only if the dimension of the image of 𝒟≤1\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1} is ℓ\ell. ∎

For a finite dimensional vector space V⊆ℛV\subseteq\mathcal{R}, we say that VV is homogeneously algebraically independent if for any basis {v1,…,vk}\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\} of VV there is no nonzero homogeneous polynomial p∈𝕂⁡[t1,…,tk]p\in\mathbb{K}[t_{1},\dots,t_{k}] such that p⁡(v1,…,vk)=0p(v_{1},\dots,v_{k})=0. We note that if this condition holds for some basis of VV, then it holds for every basis of VV. The only spaces we will consider are spaces of partial derivatives and they always contain the element 1∈ℛ1\in\mathcal{R}. Taking v1=1v_{1}=1, there is always a trivial (nonhomogeneous!) algebraic dependence p⁡(t1,…,tk)=t1−1p(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k})=t_{1}-1, so we have to restrict to homogeneous polynomials. This is mostly an aesthetic choice: if {v1=1,v2,…,vk}\{v_{1}=1,v_{2},\ldots,v_{k}\} is a basis of VV, then the homogeneous algebraic independence of VV is equivalent to the usual algebraic independence of {v2,…,vk}\{v_{2},\ldots,v_{k}\}.

Lemma 4.1.

For an encompassing polynomial, its partial derivatives are homogeneously algebraically independent.

Proof.

Fix a basis h1,…,hℓh_{1},\ldots,h_{\ell} of the space of partials, where hℓ=1h_{\ell}=1 and h1,…,hℓ−1h_{1},\ldots,h_{\ell-1} have zero constant term. By assumption, their linear terms are linearly independent, so that, possibly after a linear change, we have hi≡ximodℛ≥2h_{i}\equiv x_{i}\bmod\mathcal{R}_{\geq 2} for i=1,2,…,ℓ−1i=1,2,\ldots,\ell-1. Assume that these partials are homogeneously algebraically dependent and let Φ\Phi be a homogeneous polynomial of degree dd such that

Φ⁡(h1,…,hℓ−1,hℓ)=0.\Phi(h_{1},\ldots,h_{\ell-1},h_{\ell})=0.

Let φ:-Φ|hℓ=1\varphi\coloneq\Phi|_{h_{\ell}=1}, then φ⁡(h1,…,hℓ−1)=0\varphi(h_{1},\ldots,h_{\ell-1})=0. Let d′d^{\prime} be the smallest natural number such that φd′≠0\varphi_{d^{\prime}}\neq 0. Then

0=φd′​(ldf⁡(h1),…,ldf⁡(hℓ−1))=φd′​(x1,…,xℓ−1),0=\varphi_{d^{\prime}}\bigl(\ldf(h_{1}),\ldots,\ldf(h_{\ell-1})\bigr)=\varphi_{d^{\prime}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{\ell-1}),

so φd′\varphi_{d^{\prime}} is the zero polynomial, which is a contradiction. ∎

Proposition 4.1.

Let ff be an encompassing polynomial, let ℓ:-dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)\ell\coloneq\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f) and suppose that

ldf⁡(𝒟∘f)=⟨l0=1,l1,…,lℓ−1⟩\ldf(\mathcal{D}\circ f)=\langle l_{0}=1,l_{1},\ldots,l_{\ell-1}\rangle

for linearly independent linear forms l1,…,lℓ−1l_{1},\ldots,l_{\ell-1}. Then for every d≥1d\geq 1 we have

ldf⁡(𝒟∘fd)=𝕂​[l1,…,lℓ−1]≤d.\ldf(\mathcal{D}\circ f^{d})=\mathbb{K}[l_{1},\ldots,l_{\ell-1}]_{\leq d}.

In particular,

dim𝕂(𝒟∘fd)=(ℓ+d−1d).\dim_{\mathbb{K}}(\mathcal{D}\circ f^{d})=\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}.
Proof.

The case deg⁡(f)=0\deg(f)=0 is trivial, and in the following we assume deg⁡(f)≥1\deg(f)\geq 1. First, we simplify the notation. Change the coordinates in 𝒟=𝕂⁡[α1,…,αn]\mathcal{D}=\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}] so that the kernel of 𝒟≤1→Ap⁡(f)\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1}\to\Ap(f) is generated by αℓ,…,αn\alpha_{\ell},\ldots,\alpha_{n}. Then ff is in the subring 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xℓ−1]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{\ell-1}]. We restrict to this subring, so that nn becomes ℓ−1\ell-1 and

⟨l1,…,lℓ−1⟩=⟨x1,…,xn⟩.\langle l_{1},\ldots,l_{\ell-1}\rangle=\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle.

We make another important observation. Since 𝒟≤1\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1} surjects onto Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f), there is a linear form σ∈𝒟≤1\sigma\in\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1} such that σ∘f=1\sigma\circ f=1. Since

deg⁡(σ∘f)=0<deg⁡(f),\deg(\sigma\circ f)=0<\deg(f),

we have σ∈𝒟1\sigma\in\mathcal{D}_{1}. By changing the coordinates we can assume σ=αn\sigma=\alpha_{n}. We have

αn∘(𝒟≥1∘f)=𝒟≥1∘(αn∘f)=0,\alpha_{n}\circ(\mathcal{D}_{\geq 1}\circ f)=\mathcal{D}_{\geq 1}\circ(\alpha_{n}\circ f)=0,

so no polynomial in 𝒟≥1∘f\mathcal{D}_{\geq 1}\circ f depends on xnx_{n}. We want to prove that

ldf⁡(𝒟∘fd)=𝕂​[x1,…,xn]≤d.\ldf(\mathcal{D}\circ f^{d})=\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]_{\leq d}.

First we prove the inclusion "⊇\supseteq". Assuming that this is not the case, we have by subsection 2.6 a polynomial Φ∈Ann⁡(fd)\Phi\in\Ann(f^{d}) of degree at most dd. Let d′=deg⁡(Φ)d^{\prime}=\deg(\Phi) and let Φd′\Phi_{d^{\prime}} be its top degree form. For any 𝐚∈ℕn\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, we write α𝐚:=α1𝐚1⋯αn𝐚n\alpha^{\mathbf{a}}:=\alpha_{1}^{\mathbf{a}_{1}}\cdots\alpha_{n}^{\mathbf{a}_{n}}. Take any monomial α𝐚\alpha^{\mathbf{a}} of degree d′d^{\prime}. Then

(4.2) α𝐚∘fd=(α1𝐚1⋯αn𝐚n)∘fd≡d!(d−d′)!(α1∘f)𝐚1⋯(αn∘f)𝐚n⋅fd−d′modfd−d′+1.\alpha^{\mathbf{a}}\circ f^{d}=\left(\alpha_{1}^{\mathbf{a}_{1}}\cdots\alpha_{n}^{\mathbf{a}_{n}}\right)\circ f^{d}\equiv\frac{d!}{(d-d^{\prime})!}(\alpha_{1}\circ f)^{\mathbf{a}_{1}}\cdots(\alpha_{n}\circ f)^{\mathbf{a}_{n}}\cdot f^{d-d^{\prime}}\bmod{f^{d-d^{\prime}+1}}.

If instead α𝐚\alpha^{\mathbf{a}} has degree strictly less than d′d^{\prime}, then

α𝐚∘fd≡0modfd−d′+1.\alpha^{\mathbf{a}}\circ f^{d}\equiv 0\bmod{f^{d-d^{\prime}+1}}.

Suppose that Φd′=∑𝐚λ𝐚​α𝐚\Phi_{d^{\prime}}=\sum_{\mathbf{a}}\lambda_{\mathbf{a}}\alpha^{\mathbf{a}}. By using (4.2) repeatedly, we get

0=Φ∘fd≡Φd′∘fd≡d!(d−d′)!∑𝐚λ𝐚(α1∘f)𝐚1⋯(αn∘f)𝐚nfd−d′modfd−d′+1.0=\Phi\circ f^{d}\equiv\Phi_{d^{\prime}}\circ f^{d}\equiv\frac{d!}{(d-d^{\prime})!}\sum_{\mathbf{a}}\lambda_{\mathbf{a}}(\alpha_{1}\circ f)^{\mathbf{a}_{1}}\cdots(\alpha_{n}\circ f)^{\mathbf{a}_{n}}f^{d-d^{\prime}}\bmod{f^{d-d^{\prime}+1}}.

It follows that the sum

(4.3) ∑𝐚λ𝐚(α1∘f)𝐚1⋯(αn∘f)𝐚n\sum_{\mathbf{a}}\lambda_{\mathbf{a}}(\alpha_{1}\circ f)^{\mathbf{a}_{1}}\cdots(\alpha_{n}\circ f)^{\mathbf{a}_{n}}

is a multiple of ff. However, the sum does not depend on xnx_{n}, while every non-zero element of ℛ⋅f\mathcal{R}\cdot f depends on xnx_{n}. We obtain that the sum (4.3) is zero. By section 4 this implies Φd′≡0\Phi_{d^{\prime}}\equiv 0, which is a contradiction. This proves that Φ\Phi does not exist and hence we obtain one inclusion. The equality then follows by section 3, which completes the proof. ∎

Proof of subsection 1.2.

We begin with a preliminary remark. Since ff is concise, the map 𝒟1→Ap⁡(f)\mathcal{D}_{1}\to\Ap(f) is injective. The image of this map lies in the maximal ideal of Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f), so 𝒟≤1→Ap⁡(f)\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1}\to\Ap(f) is also injective. It follows that

(4.4) n+1=dim𝕂𝒟≤1≤dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)=ℓ.n+1=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1}\leq\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f)=\ell.

Now we begin the proof of equivalences. section 4 and section 4 prove that (4) implies (1) and (3), respectively. Let us prove that (1) implies (3). For every dd, let 𝒫d⊆ℛ\mathcal{P}_{d}\subseteq\mathcal{R} denote the linear space spanned by products ∏i=1d(σi∘f)\prod_{i=1}^{d}(\sigma_{i}\circ f) over all σi∈𝒟\sigma_{i}\in\mathcal{D}. We have a natural surjection Sd​(𝒟∘f)→𝒫dS^{d}(\mathcal{D}\circ f)\to\mathcal{P}_{d} and an inclusion 𝒟∘fd⊆𝒫d\mathcal{D}\circ f^{d}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{d}, see (3.1). Therefore

(ℓ+d−1d)=dim𝕂Sd​(𝒟∘f)≥dim𝕂𝒫d≥dim𝕂(𝒟∘fd).\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}S^{d}(\mathcal{D}\circ f)\geq\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{P}_{d}\geq\dim_{\mathbb{K}}(\mathcal{D}\circ f^{d}).

By assumption (1), equalities must hold. But the first equality shows that the map Sd​(𝒟∘f)→𝒫dS^{d}(\mathcal{D}\circ f)\to\mathcal{P}_{d} is an isomorphism, which means that the partials of ff do not satisfy any homogeneous polynomial of degree dd. Iterating over all dd, we obtain (3).

Now we prove that (3) implies (4). This is perhaps the most surprising part, because it follows easily and yet gives a strong characterization. Since the partials of ff are homogeneously algebraically independent, there are at most n+1n+1 of them, so dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)≤n+1\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f)\leq n+1. By (4.4) we have equality dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)=n+1\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f)=n+1 and additionally we get that the image of 𝒟≤1\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1} spans Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f). By section 4, this proves that ff is encompassing, hence (4).

Finally, let us prove that (2) is equivalent to (3). Assume (2). By (4.4) we have ℓ≥n+1\ell\geq n+1. By (2), we have ℓ−1≤n\ell-1\leq n. Joining these, we get ℓ=n+1\ell=n+1. Let b1,…,bℓb_{1},\ldots,b_{\ell} be a basis of the space of partials of ff, where

bi:-∂f∂𝐱i𝐚b_{i}\coloneq\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{a}}_{i}}

for i=1,2,…,ℓ−1i=1,2,\ldots,\ell-1 and bℓ=1b_{\ell}=1. Suppose that b1,…,bℓb_{1},\ldots,b_{\ell} satisfy some nonzero homogeneous polynomial Φ\Phi. Then Φ|bℓ=1\Phi|_{b_{\ell}=1} is not constant. This polynomial shows that b1,…,bℓ−1b_{1},\ldots,b_{\ell-1} are algebraically dependent. But this means that the subfield

(4.5) 𝕂⁡(b1,…,bℓ−1)⊆𝕂⁡(x1,…,xn)\mathbb{K}(b_{1},\ldots,b_{\ell-1})\subseteq\mathbb{K}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})

has transcendence degree at most ℓ−2\ell-2. However, by assumption (2), the field extension (4.5) is finite, so both fields have transcendence degree n=ℓ−1n=\ell-1. This contradiction proves (3). The proof that (3) implies (2) is analogous. ∎

4.1. Encompassing polynomial from any polynomial

In this section we discuss how to construct an encompassing polynomial from any polynomial and prove subsection 1.2. We keep the notation as in the theorem, so we are dealing with polynomial rings in kk variables, rather than in nn variables. Take a nonhomogeneous concise polynomial f∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xk]f\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}] with n:-dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)n\coloneq\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f) and fix elements

1,α1,…,αk,σ1,…,σn−k−1∈𝒟=𝕂⁡[α1,…,αk]1,\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k},\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n-k-1}\in\mathcal{D}=\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}]

restricting to a basis of Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f). Let I′:-Ann⁡(f)⊆𝒟I^{\prime}\coloneq\Ann(f)\subseteq\mathcal{D} be the annihilator of ff.

Let us now introduce the enlarged rings

ℛ^=𝕂⁡[x1,…,xk,y1,…,yn−k−1],𝒟^=𝕂⁡[α1,…,αk,β1,…,βn−k−1].\widehat{\mathcal{R}}=\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\dots,x_{k},y_{1},\dots,y_{n-k-1}],\qquad\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=\mathbb{K}[\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k},\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{n-k-1}].

We define a ring automorphism φ:𝒟^→𝒟^\varphi\colon\widehat{\mathcal{D}}\to\widehat{\mathcal{D}}, such that

φ⁡(αi)=αi,φ⁡(βj)=βj−σj,\varphi(\alpha_{i})=\alpha_{i},\quad\varphi(\beta_{j})=\beta_{j}-\sigma_{j},

for every i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k and j=1,…,n−k−1j=1,\dots,n-k-1 and consider the ideal

I:-I′⋅𝒟^+(β1−σ1,…,βn−k−1−σn−k−1)=φ⁡(Ann⁡(f)).I\coloneq I^{\prime}\cdot\widehat{\mathcal{D}}+(\beta_{1}-\sigma_{1},\dots,\beta_{n-k-1}-\sigma_{n-k-1})=\varphi\bigl(\Ann(f)\bigr).
Lemma 4.5.

The ideal II is the annihilator of an encompassing polynomial gg equal to

g=∑𝐚∈ℤ≥0n−k−1𝐲𝐚𝐚!​(σ𝐚∘f).g=\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n-k-1}}\frac{\mathbf{y}^{\mathbf{a}}}{\mathbf{a}!}(\sigma^{\mathbf{a}}\circ f).

Moreover, the apolar algebras Ap⁡(g)\Ap(g) and Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) are isomorphic.

Proof.

The algebras 𝒟^/I\widehat{\mathcal{D}}/I and 𝒟^/Ann⁡(f)≃Ap⁡(f)\widehat{\mathcal{D}}/\Ann(f)\simeq\Ap(f) are isomorphic via φ\varphi, so by Macaulay’s inverse systems (see [52]*Appendix A), we get that I=Ann⁡(g)I=\Ann(g) for some non-unique gg and Ap⁡(g)≃Ap⁡(f)\Ap(g)\simeq\Ap(f). The classes of the elements

1,α1,…,αk,−σ1,…,−σn−k−11,\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k},-\sigma_{1},\ldots,-\sigma_{n-k-1}

in 𝒟^/Ann⁡(f)\widehat{\mathcal{D}}/\Ann(f) are by definition linearly independent. Since every βj\beta_{j} annihilates ff, these classes coincide with the classes of

1,α1,…,αk,(β1−σ1),…,(βn−k−1−σn−k−1).1,\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k},(\beta_{1}-\sigma_{1}),\ldots,(\beta_{n-k-1}-\sigma_{n-k-1}).

But these are the images under φ\varphi of the classes of 1,α1,…,αk,β1,…,βn−k−11,\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k},\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{n-k-1}. Therefore, the classes of 𝒟^≤1\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{\leq 1} are linearly independent, so gg is encompassing by section 4. Finally, the explicit expression for gg, again non-unique, is given by [58]*Proposition 2.12. ∎

Example 4.5.

Let

f≔x14+x24+⋯+xn4.f\coloneqq x_{1}^{4}+x_{2}^{4}+\cdots+x_{n}^{4}.

The Hilbert function of Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) is (1,n,n,n,1)(1,n,n,n,1) and we can take

σi≔αi,σn+i≔112​αi2,σ2​n+i≔124​αi3\sigma_{i}\coloneqq\alpha_{i},\quad\sigma_{n+i}\coloneqq\frac{1}{12}\alpha_{i}^{2},\quad\sigma_{2n+i}\coloneqq\frac{1}{24}\alpha_{i}^{3}

for every i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\ldots,n, and

σ3​n+1≔124​α14.\sigma_{3n+1}\coloneqq\frac{1}{24}\alpha_{1}^{4}.

Then we have

g=f⁡(x1+y1,…,xn+yn)+∑i=1nyn+i​(yn+i+xi2)+∑i=1ny2​n+i​xi+y3​n+1.g=f(x_{1}+y_{1},\ldots,x_{n}+y_{n})+\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{n+i}(y_{n+i}+x_{i}^{2})+\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{2n+i}x_{i}+y_{3n+1}.

Unlike the examples in the introduction, here gg has parts which are quadratic in the yy-variables.

Proof of subsection 1.2.

Let a concise F∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xk]F\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{k}] and let f=F|x0=1f=F|_{x_{0}=1} is its dehomogenization. Let gg be an encompassing polynomial obtained from ff as above and let GG be its homogenization multiplied by a power of x0x_{0} so that deg⁡G=deg⁡F\deg G=\deg F and

G∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xk,y1,…,yn−k−1]≃𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn].G\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{k},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n-k-1}]\simeq\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}].

The polynomial gg restricts to ff by setting y∙=0y_{\bullet}=0, so also GG restricts to FF by setting y∙=0y_{\bullet}=0. We now observe that the homogeneous polynomial GG satisfies the assumptions of subsection 1.2. The algebra Ap⁡(g)\Ap(g) is smoothable, since it is isomorphic to Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f), and the polynomial gg is encompassing, see subsection 4.1 for both claims. This concludes this part of the proof.

Fix any dd. From subsection 1.2 it follows that the

smrk⁡(tw⁡(Gd))≤(n+dd),\smrk\bigl(\mathrm{tw}(G^{d})\bigr)\leq\binom{n+d}{d},

so we also have by (2.10) that

brk⁡(tw⁡(Gd))≤(n+dd).\brk\bigl(\mathrm{tw}(G^{d})\bigr)\leq\binom{n+d}{d}.

Since tw⁡(Fd)\mathrm{tw}(F^{d}) is a restriction of tw⁡(Gd)\mathrm{tw}(G^{d}) and border rank does not increase under restriction, we also get

brk⁡(tw⁡(Fd))≤(n+dd).\brk\bigl(\mathrm{tw}(F^{d})\bigr)\leq\binom{n+d}{d}.

Finally, the explicit form (1.2) was already noted in subsection 4.1. ∎

4.2. Almost encompassing polynomials

Definition 4.6.

A polynomial ff is almost encompassing if f≤1=0f_{\leq 1}=0 but for every nonzero element gg of 𝒟≥1∘f\mathcal{D}_{\geq 1}\circ f we have g≤1≠0g_{\leq 1}\neq 0.

For example, every quadratic form is an almost encompassing polynomial. In general, for any encompassing polynomial ff, the polynomial f≥2f_{\geq 2} is almost encompassing. This shows that many examples of almost encompassing polynomials can be produced using the method of §4.1.

In this section we show that for an almost encompassing polynomial ff, its deg⁡(f)\deg(f)-th power does not have the maximal dimension of the apolar algebra, i.e.,

dim𝕂Ap⁡(fdeg⁡f)<(deg⁡f−1+dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)deg⁡f).\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f^{\deg f})<\binom{\deg f-1+\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f)}{\deg f}.

We conclude with a similar statement for arbitrary polynomials.

Theorem 4.6.

Let ff be a non-constant polynomial with zero linear part: f1=0f_{1}=0. Then ff is equal to a polynomial of degree deg⁡f\deg f in the variables 𝒟≥1∘f\mathcal{D}_{\geq 1}\circ f.

Proof.

Take f∈ℛf\in\mathcal{R}. After a possible coordinate change and lowering the nn, we can assume that there is no linear form in the variables α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n} annihilating ff. For every j≥2j\geq 2 define a linear subspace of 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} by the formula

ℒ≥j={β∈𝒟1|∃σ∈𝒟≥j:β∘f=σ∘f}=𝒟1∩(Ann(f)+𝒟≥j).\mathcal{L}_{\geq j}=\Set{\beta\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}{\exists\,\sigma\in\mathcal{D}_{\geq j}:\beta\circ f=\sigma\circ f}=\mathcal{D}_{1}\cap\bigl(\Ann(f)+\mathcal{D}_{\geq j}\bigr).

We have inclusions

ℒ≥2⊇ℒ≥3⊇⋯⊇ℒ≥j⊇⋯,\mathcal{L}_{\geq 2}\supseteq\mathcal{L}_{\geq 3}\supseteq{\cdots}\supseteq\mathcal{L}_{\geq j}\supseteq{\cdots},

so after another coordinate change we may assume that for every jj we have an njn_{j} such that

(4.7) ℒ≥j=⟨αnj+1,…,αn⟩\mathcal{L}_{\geq j}=\langle\alpha_{n_{j}+1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\rangle

Taking k≔n2k\coloneqq n_{2} equality (4.7) for j=2j=2 shows that

Ann⁡(f)⊆⟨αk+1,…,αn⟩+𝒟≥2.\Ann(f)\subseteq\langle\alpha_{k+1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\rangle+\mathcal{D}_{\geq 2}.

Dualizing this containment, we obtain

⟨1,x1,…,xk⟩=(⟨αk+1,…,αn⟩+𝒟≥2)⟂⊆(Ann⁡(f))⟂=𝒟∘f,\langle 1,x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\rangle=\left(\langle\alpha_{k+1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\rangle+\mathcal{D}_{\geq 2}\right)^{\perp}\subseteq\bigl(\Ann(f)\bigr)^{\perp}=\mathcal{D}\circ f,

We take the degree of xix_{i} to be jj. For example, the degrees of x1,…,xkx_{1},\ldots,x_{k} are 11. We call the resulting grading on ℛ\mathcal{R} the custom grading and the degree of an element the custom degree, which we denote by deg′\deg^{\prime}.

For every i≥k+1i\geq k+1 we will now inductively generate elements σi,τi∈𝒟\sigma_{i},\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{D}. Suppose we have already generated them for all i≤nji\leq n_{j}. To get them for i=nj+1,…,nj+1i=n_{j}+1,\ldots,n_{j+1}, we use (4.7) and fix σi∈𝒟≥j\sigma_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\geq j} so that αi−σi\alpha_{i}-\sigma_{i} annihilates ff.

yn=τn∘f,…,yk+1=τk+1∘f,y_{n}=\tau_{n}\circ f,\quad\ldots,\quad y_{k+1}=\tau_{k+1}\circ f,

xi+Pi​(x1,…,xnj)x_{i}+P_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n_{j}})

Corollary 4.8.

Let ff be a polynomial in ℛ\mathcal{R} and let ℓ=dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)\ell=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f). Suppose that

dim𝕂Ap⁡(fd)=(ℓ+d−1d)\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f^{d})=\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}

for d=1,2,…,deg⁡fd=1,2,\ldots,\deg f. Then ff is encompassing.

Proof.

Suppose that ff is not encompassing. Then there is a partial g∈𝒟∘fg\in\mathcal{D}\circ f which is almost encompassing. By subsection 4.2 it follows that there is a trivial homogeneous algebraic dependence of degree d:=deg⁡(g)≤deg⁡(f)d:=\deg(g)\leq\deg(f) between the partials of ff. As in the proof of section 3 it follows that

dim𝕂Ap⁡(fd)<(ℓ+d−1d),\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f^{d})<\binom{\ell+d-1}{d},

which is a contradiction. ∎

Remark 4.8.

We conjecture that the bound in subsection 4.2 is optimal in that for every almost encompassing polynomial ff, we have

dim𝕂Ap⁡(fd)=(ℓ+d−1d)\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f^{d})=\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}

for all d<deg⁡fd<\deg f.

5. Smoothability

5.1. Smoothable rank of powers and locally encompassing polynomials

In this section we relate the previous results to the “global” setting of border ranks and smoothable ranks of homogeneous polynomials. A homogeneous polynomial F∈𝕂⁡[x0,…,xn]F\in\mathbb{K}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}] is locally encompassing if there exists a linear form, say x0x_{0}, such that F|x0=1F|_{x_{0}=1} is encompassing.

A locally encompassing form comes with the tautological apolar scheme as defined in §2.3. To complete the proof of subsection 1.2, we need to know that such a scheme is smoothable.

Example 5.0.

In the setting of subsection 1.2, we want to know that

Ap⁡((x12+…+xn−12+xn)d)\Ap\bigl((x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+x_{n-1}^{2}+x_{n})^{d}\bigr)

is smoothable for every d≥1d\geq 1. For d=1d=1 this algebra has Hilbert function HF=(1,n−2,1)\HF=(1,n-2,1) and it is smoothable, for example, by [28]*Proposition 4.9.

In fact, an explicit smoothing is given over 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} with parameter tt by the family of nn points

(0,0,…,0),(t2,t2,…,t2,12​t3),{(0,…,0,t⏟k,0,…,0)|k=1,…,n−1}.(0,0,\ldots,0),\quad\left(t^{2},t^{2},\ldots,t^{2},\frac{1}{2}t^{3}\right),\quad\Set{(\underbrace{0,\ldots,0,t}_{k},0,\dots,0)}{k=1,\ldots,n-1}.

In contrast, already for d=2d=2 the Hilbert function is

(1,n−2,(n+12)−2​n,n−2,1)\Biggl(1,n-2,\binom{n+1}{2}-2n,n-2,1\Biggr)

and there is no general statement similar to [28]*Proposition 4.9 in the literature.

For a finite dimensional 𝕂\mathbb{K}-vector space VV we have the vector spaces V⊗dV^{\otimes d} and Sd​V⊆V⊗dS^{d}V\subseteq V^{\otimes d} where Sd​V=(V⊗d)ΣdS^{d}V=(V^{\otimes d})^{\Sigma_{d}} for the usual symmetric group action. For a finite dimensional 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra AA, both A⊗dA^{\otimes d} and Sd​AS^{d}A are also algebras: the tensor product of 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebras is a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra and the symmetric group Σd\Sigma_{d} acts on A⊗dA^{\otimes d}, whence the invariants Sd​A=(A⊗d)ΣdS^{d}A=(A^{\otimes d})^{\Sigma_{d}} form its subalgebra.

Proposition 5.0.

Let AA be a smoothable 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra. Then Sd​AS^{d}A is smoothable for every d≥1d\geq 1.

Proof.

Let 𝕂⁡[[t]]→𝒜\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]\to\mathcal{A} be a smoothing of AA as in 2.8. As a 𝕂⁡[[t]]\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]-module, the algebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} is isomorphic to 𝕂​[[t]]⊕ℓ\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]^{\oplus\ell}, where ℓ=dim𝕂A\ell=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}A. Consider the tensor product algebra 𝒜⊗d\mathcal{A}^{\otimes d}. As a 𝕂⁡[[t]]\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]-module, it is free of rank ℓd\ell^{d}. The subalgebra Sd​𝒜⊆𝒜⊗dS^{d}\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{A}^{\otimes d} is stable under the 𝕂⁡[[t]]\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!] action. Power series are a principal ideal domain, so a submodule of a free 𝕂⁡[[t]]\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]-module is also free. Hence Sd​𝒜S^{d}\mathcal{A} is a free 𝕂⁡[[t]]\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!]-module.

The special fiber (Sd​𝒜)/t​Sd​𝒜(S^{d}\mathcal{A})/tS^{d}\mathcal{A} is isomorphic to Sd​AS^{d}A since Sd​(−)S^{d}(-) is exact. The generic fiber of Sd​𝒜S^{d}\mathcal{A} is isomorphic to Sd​(𝒜⁡[t−1])S^{d}(\mathcal{A}[t^{-1}]). Recall that over any field LL, a finite dimensional LL-algebra is smooth (over LL) if and only if it is étale if and only if it is geometrically reduced, that is, it is reduced and remains reduced after any change of basis by a field extension L⊆L′L\subseteq L^{\prime}, see [75]*Tag 03PC(1), Tag 030W, Tag 05DS. Take L=𝕂​[[t]]​[t−1]L=\mathbb{K}[\![t]\!][t^{-1}]. The LL-algebra

𝒜⊗d​[t−1]≃(𝒜⁡[t−1])⊗d\mathcal{A}^{\otimes d}[t^{-1}]\simeq(\mathcal{A}[t^{-1}])^{\otimes d}

is smooth by 2.8. Therefore, it is geometrically reduced, so automatically its LL-subalgebra Sd​𝒜S^{d}\mathcal{A} is also geometrically reduced, and hence it is also smooth. Thus Sd​𝒜S^{d}\mathcal{A} gives a smoothing of Sd​AS^{d}A. ∎

Proof of subsection 1.1.

The first part is proved in subsection 5.1. The second part follows from the first one and from section 3. ∎

Corollary 5.0.

Let ff be an encompassing polynomial and take ℓ=dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)\ell=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f). Suppose that Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) is smoothable. Then for every dd the algebra Ap⁡(fd)\Ap(f^{d}) is smoothable of degree (ℓ+d−1d)\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}.

Proof.

Fix any dd. Since ff is encompassing, by section 4, the algebra Ap⁡(fd)\Ap(f^{d}) has degree (ℓ+d−1d)\binom{\ell+d-1}{d}, so the claim follows from subsection 1.1. ∎

Proof of subsection 1.2.

Let ff be the encompassing dehomogenization of FF as in the theorem. Since FF was concise, also ff is concise, so the natural map 𝒟≤1→Ap⁡(f)\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1}\to\Ap(f) is injective. It is also surjective by section 4 hence it is bijective and

dim𝕂Ap⁡(f)=dim𝕂𝒟≤1=n+1.\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Ap(f)=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{D}_{\leq 1}=n+1.

By subsection 5.1 the algebra Ap⁡(fd)\Ap(f^{d}) is smoothable and of the required degree (n+dd)\binom{n+d}{d}. By subsection 2.3 the smoothable rank of FF is at most (n+dd)\binom{n+d}{d}. Moreover, by section 4 there is no polynomial of degree dd that annihilates FdF^{d}, which means that the rank of CatF,d\Cat_{F,d} is (n+dd)\binom{n+d}{d}. This shows that the smoothable rank is equal to the catalecticant rank. The border rank is always between the catalecticant rank and the smoothable rank, so it is also equal to both, and similarly for the cactus rank and the border cactus rank. ∎

Example 5.0.

In this example we show that subsection 1.2 would be false without the twists. Take the cubic form

F≔x13+x23+x0​(x1​y1+x2​y2)+x02​y0.F\coloneqq x_{1}^{3}+x_{2}^{3}+x_{0}(x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2})+x_{0}^{2}y_{0}.

The algebra Ap⁡(F|x0=1)\Ap(F|_{x_{0}=1}) is smoothable and has degree 66, so FF satisfies the assumptions of subsection 1.2. Moreover, both the smoothable and the border rank of FF are equal to 66, so that FF is not wild in the sense of [22]. The rank of the middle catalecticant for F2F^{2} is 2525, so brk⁡(F2)≥25>(72)\brk(F^{2})\geq 25>\binom{7}{2}. Similarly, brk⁡(F[2])≥25\brk(F^{[2]})\geq 25, where F[2]F^{[2]} is the divided square, see [52]*Appendix A.

Proof of subsection 1.1.

The proof follows the one of subsection 5.1, so we only sketch it. Let 𝒵=Spec⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{Z}=\Spec(\mathcal{A}) for 𝒜\mathcal{A} as in 2.8. The quotient 𝒵/⁣/G\mathcal{Z}\mathbin{\mathchoice{\left/\mkern-6.0mu\right/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}{/\mkern-5.0mu/}}G corresponds to the subalgebra 𝒜G\mathcal{A}^{G} of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. We argue as in subsection 5.1, replacing Σd\Sigma_{d}, 𝒜⊗d\mathcal{A}^{\otimes d}, Sd​𝒜S^{d}\mathcal{A} by GG, 𝒜\mathcal{A}, 𝒜G\mathcal{A}^{G}, respectively. ∎

Example 5.0.

Let

f≔x33+x1​x2​x4+x3​x42+x22​x5+x2​x3​x5+x1​x52+x53f\coloneqq x_{3}^{3}+x_{1}x_{2}x_{4}+x_{3}x_{4}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}x_{5}+x_{2}x_{3}x_{5}+x_{1}x_{5}^{2}+x_{5}^{3}

be a cubic form in 55 variables where, as always, 𝕂\mathbb{K} has characteristic zero. The algebra Ap⁡(f)\Ap(f) is smoothable by [14, 57]. It has degree 1212. The algebra Ap⁡(f2)\Ap(f^{2}) has degree 67<(12+12)67<\binom{12+1}{2}. Moreover it satisfies the trivial negative tangents condition from [59]*Theorem 1.2 and thus in particular it is not smoothable (and not cleavable).

5.2. Smoothability and border rank

It is known that the smoothability of an algebra AA corresponds to the minimal border rank of the tensor TAT_{A} (see [19, 63]). As we show below, deciding the smoothability of very simple algebras allows to determine the border rank of arbitrary tensors up to a multiplicative factor. Our results provide another indication that deciding whether an algebra is smoothable should be very hard in general.

Given a concise tensor T∈S2​(𝕂n)⊗𝕂mT\in S^{2}(\mathbb{K}^{n})\otimes\mathbb{K}^{m} and a non-negative integer kk we define the standard graded local algebra AT,kA_{T,k} as follows. The algebra AT,kA_{T,k} is nonzero only in degree 00, 11 and 22. Its degree zero part is spanned by 11. Its degree one part has a basis x1,…,xn,y1,…,ykx_{1},\dots,x_{n},y_{1},\dots,y_{k}. Its degree two part is 𝕂m\mathbb{K}^{m}. So the algebra AT,kA_{T,k} has degree 1+n+k+m1+n+k+m. Multiplication is defined as follows. Every yiy_{i} is annihilated by all variables. The multiplication between xix_{i} is defined by the linear map S2​((𝕂n)∗)→𝕂mS^{2}((\mathbb{K}^{n})^{*})\rightarrow\mathbb{K}^{m} induced by the tensor TT.

Example 5.0.

Let m=n=2m=n=2. Let TT be represented by a 22-dimensional space of symmetric 2×22\times 2 matrices:

(2​a+b3​b3​b0).\begin{pmatrix}2a+b&3b\\ 3b&0\\ \end{pmatrix}.

The multiplication tensor of the algebra AT,1A_{T,1}, represented as a linear space of symmetric matrices, is:

(jx1x2y1abx12​a+b3​b000x23​b0000y100000a00000b00000).\begin{pNiceMatrix}j&x_{1}&x_{2}&y_{1}&a&b\\ x_{1}&2a+b&3b&0&0&0\\ x_{2}&3b&0&0&0&0\\ y_{1}&0&0&0&0&0\\ a&0&0&0&0&0\\ b&0&0&0&0&0\end{pNiceMatrix}.
Definition 5.1.

In analogy to the usual rank, for tensors T∈S2​(𝕂n)⊗𝕂mT\in S^{2}(\mathbb{K}^{n})\otimes\mathbb{K}^{m} we define partially symmetric rank of TT as the minimum rr so that TT is a sum of rr rank one tensors in S2​(𝕂n)⊗𝕂mS^{2}(\mathbb{K}^{n})\otimes\mathbb{K}^{m}. For 𝕂=ℂ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}, the partially symmetric border rank of TT is the minimum rr so that in every neighbourhood of TT there are tensors of partially symmetric rank rr.

Proposition 5.1.

For any k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, any tensor T∈S2​(𝕂n)⊗𝕂mT\in S^{2}(\mathbb{K}^{n})\otimes\mathbb{K}^{m} is a restriction of the tensor TAT,kT_{A_{T,k}} of the algebra AT,kA_{T,k} associated to TT. In particular, the border rank of TT is at most the border rank of TAT,kT_{A_{T,k}}. If AT,kA_{T,k} is smoothable, then the border rank and the partially symmetric border rank of TT are at most 1+n+k+m1+n+k+m.

At first glance, setting k=0k=0 seems optimal. However, it may well happen that AT,0A_{T,0} is not smoothable, while AT,kA_{T,k} is smoothable for some k>0k>0.

Proof.

The tensor TT is a restriction since it corresponds to the multiplication map of two elements of degree one in AT,kA_{T,k}. If AA is a tuple of ee points, then TAT_{A} has partially symmetric rank ee, so if AT,kA_{T,k} is smoothable then TAT,kT_{A_{T,k}} has partially symmetric border rank dim𝕂AT,k=1+n+k+m\dim_{\mathbb{K}}A_{T,k}=1+n+k+m. The last statement follows. ∎

Theorem 5.1.

If TT has partially symmetric border rank bb, then AT,b−mA_{T,b-m} is smoothable.

Remark 5.1.

Note that for any T∈S2​(𝕂n)⊗𝕂mT\in S^{2}(\mathbb{K}^{n})\otimes\mathbb{K}^{m} we may consider an isomorphic nonconcise tensor T′∈S2​(𝕂n)⊗𝕂m+1T^{\prime}\in S^{2}(\mathbb{K}^{n})\otimes\mathbb{K}^{m+1}. For such a tensor we have AT,k+1=AT′,kA_{T,k+1}=A_{T^{\prime},k}. Hence, formally AT,b−m=AT′,b−(m+1)A_{T,b-m}=A_{T^{\prime},b-(m+1)}, whenever b−(m+1)≥0b-(m+1)\geq 0. Thus, we can naturally extend the definition of AT,b−mA_{T,b-m}, even when b−m<0b-m<0, which may happen only for non-concise tensors. This reduces the theorem to the case where TT is concise.

Proof.

A family of TT induces a flat family of AT,b−mA_{T,b-m}, so by semicontinuity it suffices to prove the result for TT of partially symmetric rank equal to bb. Such a tensor TT is given by ∑i=1bLi⊗2⊗zi\sum_{i=1}^{b}L_{i}^{\otimes 2}\otimes z_{i}, where Li∈𝕂nL_{i}\in\mathbb{K}^{n} and zi∈𝕂mz_{i}\in\mathbb{K}^{m} are arbitrary. Since TT has partially symmetric rank bb, the LiL_{i} are pairwise different. Consider a generic tensor of such rank: let T′∈S2​(𝕂n)⊗𝕂bT^{\prime}\in S^{2}(\mathbb{K}^{n})\otimes\mathbb{K}^{b} be given by

T′=∑i=1bLi2⊗zi~,T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{b}L_{i}^{2}\otimes\widetilde{z_{i}},

where z1~,…,zb~\widetilde{z_{1}},\ldots,\widetilde{z_{b}} is a basis of 𝕂b\mathbb{K}^{b}. Then TT is a restriction of T′T^{\prime} by a linear map π\pi which sends every zi~\widetilde{z_{i}} to ziz_{i}. This map has an mm-dimensional image by the assumption on the conciseness of TT. Let K=ker⁡π⊆𝕂bK=\ker\pi\subseteq\mathbb{K}^{b} and let k1,…,kb−mk_{1},\ldots,k_{b-m} be the basis of KK.

(ki−λ​yi|i=1,…,b−m).\left(k_{i}-\lambda y_{i}\ |\ i=1,\ldots,b-m\right).

We will now prove that AT′,0A_{T^{\prime},0} is smoothable, so BT​(λ)B_{T}(\lambda) is smoothable for λ≠0\lambda\neq 0 and, by semicontinuity (see subsection 1.1) BT​(λ=0)≃AT,b−mB_{T}(\lambda=0)\simeq A_{T,b-m} is also smoothable.

Recall that AT′,0A_{T^{\prime},0} is generated by x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n} and its degree two part is identified with 𝕂b\mathbb{K}^{b}, where the multiplication is induced by L1⊗2L_{1}^{\otimes 2}, …, Lb⊗2L_{b}^{\otimes 2}. Every form Li∈⟨x1,…,xn⟩∗L_{i}\in\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle^{*} yields a point of the affine space 𝔸n=Spec⁡𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{A}^{n}=\Spec\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. Consider, for every μ∈𝕂\mu\in\mathbb{K} the subscheme of 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} given by

{μ​L1}∪{μ​L2}∪…∪{μ​Lb}∪Spec⁡(𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn](x1,…,xn)2).\{\mu L_{1}\}\cup\left\{\mu L_{2}\right\}\cup\ldots\cup\left\{\mu L_{b}\right\}\cup\Spec\left(\frac{\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]}{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})^{2}}\right).

Corollary 5.1.

For a tensor T∈S2​(𝕂n)⊗𝕂mT\in S^{2}(\mathbb{K}^{n})\otimes\mathbb{K}^{m} let kk be the smallest integer such that AT,kA_{T,k} is smoothable. Then the partially symmetric border rank of TT is at most 1+n+k1+n+k and at least kk.

Proof.

The first estimate follows from subsection 5.2 and the second from subsection 5.2. ∎

Definition 5.2.

For any concise tensor T∈𝕂n⊗𝕂n⊗𝕂mT\in\mathbb{K}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{m} let TS∈S2​(𝕂2​n)⊗𝕂mT_{S}\in S^{2}(\mathbb{K}^{2n})\otimes\mathbb{K}^{m} be constructed by replacing each slice T⁡(ej∗)T(e_{j}^{*}) by a symmetric 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n matrix, placing T⁡(ej∗)T(e_{j}^{*}) on the antidiagonal blocks, where one block is transposed in order to obtain symmetry. Clearly, TST_{S} restricts to TT.

Corollary 5.2.

For a concise T∈𝕂n⊗𝕂n⊗𝕂mT\in\mathbb{K}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{m} let kk be the smallest integer such that ATS,kA_{T_{S},k} is smoothable. Then the border rank of TT is at most 1+2​n+k1+2n+k and at least 12​k\frac{1}{2}k.

Proof.

As TST_{S} restricts to TT, the partially symmetric border rank of TST_{S} is at least the border rank of TT. We claim that the partially symmetric border rank of TST_{S} is at most twice the border rank of TT.Considering the limits, it suffices to consider the case where TT has rank rr, i.e. T=∑j=1rxj⊗yj⊗zjT=\sum_{j=1}^{r}x_{j}\otimes y_{j}\otimes z_{j}. We have:

2​TS=∑j=1r(yj,xj)⊗2⊗zj+∑j=1r(i​yj,−i​xj)⊗2⊗zj.2T_{S}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}(y_{j},x_{j})^{\otimes 2}\otimes z_{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{r}(iy_{j},-ix_{j})^{\otimes 2}\otimes z_{j}.

So if the rank of TT is rr then the partially symmetric rank of TST_{S} is at most 2​r2r.

The claim follows by applying subsection 5.2 to TST_{S}. ∎

This implies that efficient, general criteria for proving nonsmoothability of simple algebras could lead to superlinear in nn lower bounds on the border rank of tensors. Further, efficient, general criteria for proving smoothability of simple algebras could lead to upper bounds on the asymptotic rank and the exponent [60] of any tensor up to arbitrary precision. This indicates that obtaining both types of criteria is extremely difficult. However, for further detail, we refer to [59].

The lower estimate 12​k\frac{1}{2}k in subsection 5.2 makes us lose a multiplicative constant 12\frac{1}{2}. This is due to the fact that we insisted on staying in the realm of algebras and had to symmetrize our tensor. By working with 1A1_{A}-generic tensors instead, we get results that are more efficient. Recall that 1A1_{A}-generic tensors T∈𝕂a⊗𝕂b⊗𝕂bT\in\mathbb{K}^{a}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{b}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{b} of minimal border rank bb correspond to smoothable modules and are actively studied [63, 79, 56, 55].

Proposition 5.2.

For any concise tensor T∈𝕂a⊗𝕂b⊗𝕂cT\in\mathbb{K}^{a}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{b}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{c} of border rank kk there exists a concise, 1𝕂a+11_{\mathbb{K}^{a+1}}-generic, minimal border rank b+kb+k tensor T′∈𝕂a+1⊗𝕂b+k⊗𝕂b+kT^{\prime}\in\mathbb{K}^{a+1}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{b+k}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{b+k} such that TT is a restriction of T′T^{\prime}. where the entries of T⁡((𝕂c)∗)T\bigl((\mathbb{K}^{c})^{*}\bigr) are linear forms in z1,…,zcz_{1},\dots,z_{c}.

Proof.

We proceed by analogy with the proof of subsection 5.2. However, as we are no longer in the realm of algebras, we provide our rank and border rank estimates in a more direct way.

If Ti→TT_{i}\rightarrow T, then Ti′→T′T_{i}^{\prime}\rightarrow T^{\prime}. Thus, it is enough to prove the statement under the assumption that TT has rank kk. Let T=∑j=1kaj⊗bj⊗cjT=\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_{j}\otimes b_{j}\otimes c_{j}. Let T~\widetilde{T} be the corresponding generic tensor, i.e. T~=∑j=1kaj⊗bj⊗c~j\widetilde{T}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_{j}\otimes b_{j}\otimes\widetilde{c}_{j}, where c~j\widetilde{c}_{j} form a basis of 𝕂k\mathbb{K}^{k}.     bb matrices NjN_{j}, for j=1,…,bj=1,\dots,b, with a non-zero entry in the first row and column jj.

    Mn,j=(1,1n​aj)⊗((n⋅bj)+eb+j),M_{n,j}=\biggl(1,\frac{1}{n}a_{j}\biggr)\otimes\left((n\cdot b_{j})+e_{b+j}\right),

    and eb+je_{b+j} is the (b+j)(b+j)-th basis vector of 𝕂b+k\mathbb{K}^{b+k}.

For every ei∗∈(𝕂c)∗e_{i}^{*}\in(\mathbb{K}^{c})^{*} the layer ei∗​(T)e_{i}^{*}(T) is a linear combination of aj⊗bja_{j}\otimes b_{j}, so of ej∗​(T~)e_{j}^{*}(\widetilde{T}). Corollary 5.2.

Fix a concise tensor T∈𝕂a⊗𝕂b⊗𝕂cT\in\mathbb{K}^{a}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{b}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{c}. Let kk be the smallest integer, so that the tensor T′T^{\prime} from the statement of subsection 5.2 has border rank b+kb+k. Then TT has border rank at least kk and at most b+kb+k.

6. Sweet pieces

In this section we define a class of tensors that we call sweet pieces. As we will argue, sweet pieces play an essential role when using the Coppersmith-Winograd method to bound the constant ω\omega that governs the complexity of matrix multiplication. Surprisingly, as we will see, sweet pieces have rank strictly smaller than the bounds used so far in the CW-method. The introduction of sweet pieces also allows to remove any reference to border rank and the Coppersmith-Winograd tensor to obtain upper bounds on ω\omega, as in [35]. We start by recalling notions from complexity theory. A good reference for the methods we describe is [25]*Part IV. We work over 𝕂\mathbb{K}, which as before is algebraically closed and of characteristic zero. Much of the literature below is done only for ℂ\mathbb{C}. If necessary, we can always reduce to this case, by restricting 𝕂\mathbb{K} to a countably generated field (containing all coefficients of all involved tensors etc.) and embedding it into ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Definition 6.1.

Given three vector spaces V1V_{1}, V2V_{2}, and V3V_{3}, for a tensor T∈V1⊗V2⊗V3T\in V_{1}\otimes V_{2}\otimes V_{3}, a blocking is a triad of functions fi:ℬi→ℤrf_{i}\colon\mathcal{B}_{i}\to\mathbb{Z}^{r}, where ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} is a basis of ViV_{i} for every i=1,2,3i=1,2,3. For any (a1,a2,a3)∈(ℤr)3(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3})\in(\mathbb{Z}^{r})^{3}, a block Ta1,a2,a3T_{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}} is the image of TT by the projection

V1⊗V2⊗V3→V1′⊗V2′⊗V3′,V_{1}\otimes V_{2}\otimes V_{3}\rightarrow V_{1}^{\prime}\otimes V_{2}^{\prime}\otimes V_{3}^{\prime},

where Vi′⊂ViV_{i}^{\prime}\subset V_{i} is defined as the linear subspace

Vi′≔⟨{b∈ℬi|fi​(b)=ai}⟩.V_{i}^{\prime}\coloneqq\langle\Set{b\in\mathcal{B}_{i}}{f_{i}(b)=a_{i}}\rangle.

A block is said to be in the support of the tensor, if it is nonzero. A tensor with a blocking (f1,f2,f3)(f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}) is said to be tight if for every block (a1,a2,a3)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}) in the support, a1+a2+a3=0∈ℤra_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}=0\in\mathbb{Z}^{r}.

Sometimes we will write block (a1,a2,a3)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}), instead of Ta1,a2,a3T_{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}.

Remark 6.1.

In the literature one either refers to:

  • •

    tight tensors, assuming one can choose bases of each ViV_{i} and the blocking is given by injective functions, i.e., the blocks are 1×1×11\times 1\times 1 tensors [34], or

  • •

    tight sets; in our case, this corresponds to fixing bases of the vector spaces V1,V2,V3V_{1},V_{2},V_{3} [26, Section 15.7].

The definition above is flexible enough to easily interpolate between these two.

By a (probability) distribution pp on any set SS we mean a function p:S→ℝ≥0p:S\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, such that

∑s∈Sp⁡(s)=1.\sum_{s\in S}p(s)=1.

Thus, a probability distribution pp on the support SS of a tensor TT with fixed blocking assigns a non-negative real number p⁡(a,b,c)p(a,b,c) to each (a,b,c)(a,b,c) indexing a block in the support of TT. Such a distribution induces three marginal distributions p1,p2,p3p_{1},p_{2},p_{3}, where pip_{i} is a distribution on the image of fif_{i}. More precisely,

p1​(a)≔∑(a,b,c)∈Sp⁡(a,b,c)p_{1}(a)\coloneqq\sum_{(a,b,c)\in S}p(a,b,c)

and similarly for p2p_{2} and p3p_{3}.

The following definition has appeared implicitly in many articles on fast matrix multiplication. While it looks technical, in practice it means that the tensor is sufficiently symmetric so that it shares many properties with a tensor that is simply a direct sum of copies of the same tensor.

Definition 6.2.

A sweet piece is a tight tensor TT, with a fixed blocking f1,f2,f3f_{1},f_{2},f_{3} such that:

  1. (1)

    each block in the support is isomorphic to a fixed tensor UU;

  2. (2)

    the uniform distribution on support has three equal marginals, which are also uniform.

The cardinality of the image of each fif_{i}, which by the definition does not depend on ii, is denoted by pTp_{T}.

Definition 6.3.

For a tensor TT its asymptotic rank is defined by

limn→∞R​(T⊠n)1n,\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}R(T^{\boxtimes n})^{\frac{1}{n}},

where R⁡(T⊠n)R(T^{\boxtimes n}) is the rank of the nn-th Kronecker power of TT. For a concise tensor T∈𝕂a⊗𝕂b⊗𝕂cT\in\mathbb{K}^{a}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{b}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{c} the asymptotic rank is always greater than or equal to max⁡(a,b,c)\max(a,b,c) and we say that a tensor has minimal asymptotic rank if equality holds.

For example, the 2×22\times 2 matrix multiplication tensor M2M_{2} has asymptotic rank 2ω2^{\omega}. The following theorem can be considered as the cornerstone of the Coppersmith-Winograd method.

Theorem 6.3.

Let T∈(𝕂pT​a2)⊗3T\in(\mathbb{K}^{p_{T}a^{2}})^{\otimes 3} be a sweet piece of asymptotic rank rr, with blocking (f1,f2,f3)(f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}), where each block UU is isomorphic to the matrix multiplication tensor MaM_{a}, with a>1a>1. Then

ω≤loga⁡(r/pT)=loga⁡(r/|im⁡fi|).\omega\leq\log_{a}(r/p_{T})=\log_{a}(r/|\im f_{i}|).

In particular, if TT has minimal asymptotic rank, then ω=2\omega=2.

Proof.

Consider the uniform probability distribution for all blocks and apply the main Coppersmith-Winograd theorem, for example as in [25]*Theorem 15.41. ∎

The proof above suggests that section 6 is a simple consequence of the results of Coppersmith and Winogrand. However, we want to emphasize that sweet pieces play an absolutely central role in the whole theory. In particular, the main part of [35] can be restated as the following lemma.

Lemma 6.3.

Let TT be a sweet piece and ε>0\varepsilon>0. There exists N≫0N\gg 0, such that T⊠NT^{\boxtimes N} restricts to ⌊(pT−ε)⌋N\lfloor(p_{T}-\varepsilon)\rfloor^{N} disjoint copies of U⊠NU^{\boxtimes N}.

We emphasize that in section 6 we do not need to degenerate the tensor to get a direct sum

(U⊠N)⊕⌊(pT−ε)⌋N,(U^{\boxtimes N})^{\oplus\lfloor(p_{T}-\varepsilon)\rfloor^{N}},

but only to restrict it11 1 However, the proof that such a restriction exists is not constructive and relies on probabilistic arguments..

The CW-method also provides a way to create new sweet pieces. One starts with a tight tensor TT, with blocking f1,f2,f3f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}, and a probability distribution PP on the support of TT. Note that the blocking on TT induces the blocking on T⊠NT^{\boxtimes N}, where the indices of the blocks are sequences of length NN of indices for blocks of TT. In particular, each block BB in T⊠NT^{\boxtimes N} provides three sequences of length NN. The ii-th sequence gives a probability distribution pi​(B)p_{i}(B) on the image of fif_{i}, where the probability of a∈im⁡fia\in\im f_{i} is equal to the number of times aa appears in the ii-th sequence divided by NN.

Proposition 6.3.

Let TT be a tight tensor with a fixed blocking. Assume PP is a probability distribution on blocks bb in the support of TT that is reconstructable from its three marginals22 2 i.e. it is the unique probability distribution on the support with given marginals and all three marginals are the same distributions. Assume that NN is such an integer that N​pNp is integral. Then, the projection of T⊠NT^{\boxtimes N} onto the basis vectors belonging to the blocks BB, such that for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3 the ii-th marginal of PP is pi​(B)p_{i}(B), is a sweet piece.

Proof.

Since the three marginals for TT are the same, by the action of the permutation group ΣN\Sigma_{N} on the entries of the indexing sequences and the action of Σ3\Sigma_{3} on the sequences themselves, the second point in 6.2 holds. We have to prove that all blocks in the support are isomorphic. Indeed, we claim that each one is isomorphic to the Kronecker product of NN blocks of TT, where each block bb appears P⁡(b)​NP(b)N many times. Fix a block BB in T⊠NT^{\boxtimes N}, indexed by the three sequences

(a1,…,aN),(a1′,…,aN′),(a1′′,…,aN′′).(a_{1},\dots,a_{N}),\quad(a_{1}^{\prime},\dots,a_{N}^{\prime}),\quad(a_{1}^{\prime\prime},\dots,a_{N}^{\prime\prime}).

Then BB is isomorphic to the Kronecker product of Tai,ai′,ai′′T_{a_{i},a_{i}^{\prime},a_{i}^{\prime\prime}} i.e. blocks of TT indexed by ai,ai′,ai′′a_{i},a_{i}^{\prime},a_{i}^{\prime\prime}. The three sequences provide a probability distribution P′P^{\prime} on the support blocks of TT. By the choice of the projection, P′P^{\prime} and PP have the same marginals. By the assumption on PP, we have P=P′P=P^{\prime} and the claim follows. ∎

The sweet piece of section 6 is denoted by S​P​(T)SP(T) or S​PP,N​(T)SP_{P,N}(T). Even if TT is not tight, as we will see, the same construction, via projection of Kronecker powers, may lead to sweet pieces. Let T∈V1⊗V2⊗V3T\in V_{1}\otimes V_{2}\otimes V_{3} be a (possibly not tight) tensor with a fixed blocking. Fix a 𝕂∗\mathbb{K}^{*} action on each ViV_{i}, where the fixed basis vectors are eigenvectors and the weight w⁡(e)=w⁡(fi​(e))w(e)=w\bigl(f_{i}(e)\bigr) of the action on a basis vector ee depends only on fi​(e)f_{i}(e). We obtain induced weights of blocks, where the block indexed by (a1,a2,a3)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}) has weight

w⁡(a1)+w⁡(a2)+w⁡(a3).w(a_{1})+w(a_{2})+w(a_{3}).

Assume that for non-zero blocks the weights are non-negative. Let T′T^{\prime} be the toric degeneration of TT, with the parameter 𝕂∗∋t→0\mathbb{K}^{*}\ni t\rightarrow 0.

Lemma 6.3.

Using the notation introduced above, assume that the toric degeneration T′T^{\prime} satisfies the assumptions of section 6. If S​P​(T′)≠0SP(T^{\prime})\neq 0, then S​P​(T)=S​P​(T′)SP(T)=SP(T^{\prime}).

Proof.

Clearly, S​P​(T)SP(T) and S​P​(T′)SP(T^{\prime}) agree on blocks where S​P​(T′)SP(T^{\prime}) is not zero. So it remains to show that if a block is zero in S​P​(T′)SP(T^{\prime}), then it is also zero in S​P​(T)SP(T). Pick a zero block in S​P​(T′)SP(T^{\prime}) indexed by three sequences. By contradiction, assume that this block is non-zero in S​P​(T)SP(T). Consider the probability distribution PP on the blocks of TT induced by the three sequences. As the block was nonzero in S​P​(T)SP(T) and zero in S​P​(T′)SP(T^{\prime}), the probability distribution must be supported on blocks of non-negative weight in TT and positive on at least one block of positive weight. Let P′P^{\prime} be the probability distribution on the blocks of TT induced by the three sequences labeling a block in the support of S​P​(T′)SP(T^{\prime}). Note that PP and P′P^{\prime} have the same marginals. Thus, P−P′P-P^{\prime} is negative only on blocks with weight zero, is positive on at least one block with positive weight and has all three marginals equal to zero.

Let SS be the sum of the weights of all the blocks, each one multiplied by the value P−P′P-P^{\prime} attains on that block. Looking at the marginals, we see that S=0S=0. However, by summing over all the blocks we see that S>0S>0, which is a contradiction and concludes the proof. ∎

Definition 6.4.

Let GG be a finite abelian group. We identify GG with the basis of 𝕂G\mathbb{K}^{G}. We define TG∈𝕂G⊗𝕂G⊗𝕂GT_{G}\in\mathbb{K}^{G}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{G}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{G} in this basis by

TG:=∑g1+g2=g3∈Gg1⊗g2⊗g3.T_{G}:=\sum_{g_{1}+g_{2}=g_{3}\in G}g_{1}\otimes g_{2}\otimes g_{3}.

By the discrete Fourier transform this is a tensor of rank |G||G| and thus is isomorphic to the unit tensor. The tensor C​Wn∈𝕂n⊗𝕂n⊗𝕂nCW_{n}\in\mathbb{K}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{K}^{n} is defined as

C​Wn:-∑i=1ne1⊗ei⊗ei+∑i=2nei⊗e1⊗ei+∑i=2n−1ei⊗ei⊗en.CW_{n}\coloneq\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_{1}\otimes e_{i}\otimes e_{i}+\sum_{i=2}^{n}e_{i}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{i}+\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}e_{i}\otimes e_{i}\otimes e_{n}.

The next lemma and corollary can be seen as variants or special cases of [2] and [48]*Proposition 4.1. The first paper explicitly states that TGT_{G} can replace C​W|G|CW_{|G|} for the bounds on ω\omega. In the second, the authors provide degenerations of a larger class of tensors to C​WnCW_{n}. The main difference with the second article is that we can identify sweet pieces of two tensors. Unlike the first article, we can later apply our results to obtain new rank estimates of the sweet pieces of both tensors.

Lemma 6.4.

For any abelian group GG of cardinality at least three, the structure tensor TGT_{G} has a 𝕂∗\mathbb{K}^{*} degeneration into the big Coppersmith-Winograd tensor C​W|G|CW_{|G|}, by using the blocking as in [35].

Proof.

Let g∈Gg\in G be a non-neutral element. Assign weight 00 to the neutral element, weight 11 to all elements different from gg and the neutral element, and weight 22 to gg for the first two copies of 𝕂G\mathbb{K}^{G} and minus these weights for the third copy. The toric degeneration is isomorphic to C​W|G|CW_{|G|}. ∎

Corollary 6.4.

The tensors TGT_{G} and C​W|G|CW_{|G|} have the same sweet pieces. In particular, S​PN​(C​Wn)SP_{N}(CW_{n}) has rank at most nNn^{N}.

The above corollary allows us to get better bounds for the rank of S​P​(C​Wn)SP(CW_{n}).

Definition 6.5.

Let TT be a tensor with a blocking and a probability distribution PP on the blocks. A chimney is the image of T⊠NT^{\boxtimes N} under the projection map:

V1⊗N⊗V2⊗N⊗V3⊗N→V1′⊗V2′⊗V3⊗N,V_{1}^{\otimes N}\otimes V_{2}^{\otimes N}\otimes V_{3}^{\otimes N}\rightarrow V_{1}^{\prime}\otimes V_{2}^{\prime}\otimes V_{3}^{\otimes N},

where, for i=1,2i=1,2, the subspace Vi′V_{i}^{\prime} is spanned only by basis vectors indexed by sequences that produce the same probability distribution as the ii-th marginal of PP. By changing i=1,2i=1,2 to i=1,3i=1,3 or i=2,3i=2,3 we get two other similar chimneys.

Note that if we think of T⊠NT^{\boxtimes N} as a three-dimensional cuboid, we should think of the sweet piece as the intersection of three chimneys.

Proposition 6.5.

Consider a probability distribution on the six blocks in the support of C​WnCW_{n} that assigns pp to each of the three large blocks of format (n−2)2×1(n-2)^{2}\times 1 and q=1/3−pq=1/3-p to each of the three small blocks of format 131^{3}. The rank of S​PN,P​(C​Wn)SP_{N,P}(CW_{n}) is smaller than

nN−(N23​N+1)​(n−1)13​N−1.n^{N}-\binom{N}{\frac{2}{3}N+1}(n-1)^{\frac{1}{3}N-1}.

In particular, it is smaller than border rank of (C​Wn)⊠N(CW_{n})^{\boxtimes N}.

Proof.

By section 6 it is enough to prove the statement for S​PN,P​(TG)SP_{N,P}(T_{G}) for |G|=n|G|=n. Note that (TG)⊠N(T_{G})^{\boxtimes N} is a tensor of minimal rank nNn^{N}.

Let us consider the corresponding chimney with entries indexed by triples of sequences of group elements, where for the first two sequences the neutral element appears (p+2​q)​N(p+2q)N times and the distinguished group element g∈Gg\in G appears q​NqN times. Note that the third sequence is arbitrary, as we are working with the chimney, not the sweet piece.

Note also that an entry in the chimney indexed by (gi),(gi′),(gi′′)(g_{i}),(g_{i}^{\prime}),(g_{i}^{\prime\prime}) is nonzero only if: for any i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N we have the implication: if gi=eg_{i}=e then gi′=gi′′g_{i}^{\prime}=g_{i}^{\prime\prime}. In particular, as we have (p+2​q)​N(p+2q)N neutral elements in the first sequence and only q​NqN elements equal to gg in the second sequence, the entries are always zero if the third sequence contains less than (p+q)​N(p+q)N elements distinct from gg. In particular, there are at least

(N(2​p+2​q)​N+1)​(n−1)(p+q)​N−1=(N23​N+1)​(n−1)13​N−1\binom{N}{(2p+2q)N+1}(n-1)^{(p+q)N-1}=\binom{N}{\frac{2}{3}N+1}(n-1)^{\frac{1}{3}N-1}

sequences indexing layers of the chimney that have only zero entries.

We now apply the classical substitution method ([63]*§3, [71]) for the tensor (TG)⊠N(T_{G})^{\boxtimes N} and the layers that are zero in the chimney. Note that we do not change the sweet piece, since the layers, that are nonzero in the whole tensor, are zero over the sweet piece. The result follows. ∎

Remark 6.5.

Clearly, the previous estimate can be made much better. We believe that estimating the ranks and the border ranks of sweet pieces may lead to new discoveries about the bounds on ω\omega. We also emphasize that if we bound the ranks of sweet pieces, all the barrier results, as in [32] do not apply. In particular, it is in principle possible to prove ω=2\omega=2, even using arbitrarily large Coppersmith-Winograd tensors, provided we find better bounds on the ranks of sweet pieces.

Our next aim is to explain relations between sweet pieces and smoothability of algebras. We note that C​WnCW_{n} is the structure tensor of the algebra AA apolar to the quadric

f≔x12+⋯+xn−22.f\coloneqq x_{1}^{2}+\dots+x_{n-2}^{2}.

Hence, C​Wn⊠NCW_{n}^{\boxtimes N} is the structure tensor of the algebra A⊗NA^{\otimes N} apolar to f⊠Nf^{\boxtimes N}. We note that AA comes with the standard grading and has Hilbert function (1,n−2,1)(1,n-2,1). Thus A⊗NA^{\otimes N} is multigraded and with respect to the total grading

dim𝕂(A⊗N)i=∑j=0⌊i2⌋(Nj)​(N−ji−2​j)​(n−2)i−2​j.\dim_{\mathbb{K}}(A^{\otimes N})_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor\frac{i}{2}\rfloor}\binom{N}{j}\binom{N-j}{i-2j}(n-2)^{i-2j}.

The grading on AA corresponds exactly to the blocking of C​WnCW_{n} introduced in [35]. The total grading on C​Wn⊠NCW_{n}^{\boxtimes N} corresponds to the blocking on Kronecker powers of this tensor, which has been used most often so far.

Lemma 6.5.

Let TT be a structure tensor of a graded algebra AA, with the blocking induced by the grading. Consider the total grading on A⊗NA^{\otimes N}. Let PP be a probability distribution on the blocks of TT that is reconstructible from its marginals P1P_{1}, P2P_{2}, P3P_{3} that have the same distribution. Let NN be such an integer that N⋅PN\cdot P is integral. Then, there exists a degree ii, such that S​PP,N​(T)SP_{P,N}(T) is a restriction of the tensor representing the map:

(A⊗N)i×(A⊗N)i→(A⊗N)2​i.(A^{\otimes N})_{i}\times(A^{\otimes N})_{i}\rightarrow(A^{\otimes N})_{2i}.
Proof.

An indexing sequence of NN elements of AA is an indexing sequence for the first coordinate in S​P​(T)SP(T) if and only if elements of degree dd appear P1​(d)​NP_{1}(d)N times in it. Thus the total degree of such a sequence is i:=∑dP1​(d)​d​Ni:=\sum_{d}P_{1}(d)dN. ∎

In the setting of the previous lemma S​P​(T)SP(T) may also be seen as a restriction of the tensor that is the structure tensor of the subalgebra of A⊗NA^{\otimes N} generated in degree ii. Such algebras are in most cases of much smaller dimension, even asymptotically with NN.

Example 6.5.

Let A=𝕂⁡[x,y]/(x2,y2)A=\mathbb{K}[x,y]/(x^{2},y^{2}) be the algebra representing the C​W4CW_{4} tensor. Let PP be the probability distribution equal to 1/31/3 on the large blocks of the support of format 22×12^{2}\times 1. The Veronese subalgebra of A⊗3​kA^{\otimes 3k} generated in degree kk has dimension

2+2​∑a=0k(3​ka)⋅(3​k−a2​k−a).2+2\sum_{a=0}^{k}\binom{3k}{a}\cdot\binom{3k-a}{2k-a}.

The sweet piece S​PP,3​k​(C​W4)SP_{P,3k}(CW_{4}) is a subtensor of the tensor associated to that Veronese algebra.

One way to realize the Veronese subalgebra of A⊗NA^{\otimes N} generated in degree ii is to fix a Gi:=ℤ/i​ℤG_{i}:=\mathbb{Z}/i\mathbb{Z} action on AA, where elements of degree one are acted upon with 1∈Gi1\in G_{i}. We can also think of it as multiplication by the complex ii-th root of unity. Then the Veronese subalgebra we are interested in is given by the invariants (A⊗N)Gi(A^{\otimes N})^{G_{i}}. Unfortunately, as we have seen in subsection 1.1, even if AA is smoothable and so is A⊗NA^{\otimes N}, the algebra of invariants does not have to be.

Let T∈(𝕂n)⊗3T\in(\mathbb{K}^{n})^{\otimes 3} be a tensor giving rise to sweet piece S​P​(T)SP(T), where each block is a matrix multiplication tensor. Note that the only asymptotically non-optimal estimation in the Coppersmith-Winograd method is precisely the point where the size of T⊗NT^{\otimes N}, that is nNn^{N}, is usually much larger than the size of S​P​(T)SP(T). In particular, either

  • •

    if S​P​(T)SP(T) grows in size as nNn^{N}, as it is the case for the symmetric tensor T∈(𝕂3)⊗3T\in(\mathbb{K}^{3})^{\otimes 3} given by the monomial x​y​zxyz, and TT is of minimal asymptotic rank (cf. [25, Remark 15.44]), or

  • •

    if one can prove that S​P​(T)SP(T) has minimal asymptotic rank,

then ω=2\omega=2, by section 6. Further, asymptotically in NN improvements on the (asymptotic) border rank of (A⊗N)Gi(A^{\otimes N})^{G_{i}} would lead to improvements on the bounds on ω\omega.

In the last part of the article we exhibit relations of sweet pieces to NP-hard problems in complexity theory. Consider the algebra B:=𝕂⁡[x]/(x2)B:=\mathbb{K}[x]/(x^{2}) and let TB∈(𝕂2)⊗3T_{B}\in(\mathbb{K}^{2})^{\otimes 3} be the associated tensor. It is natural to identify a basis of 𝕂2\mathbb{K}^{2} with subsets of the set with one element. Thus the tensor TBT_{B} has the three entries equal to one exactly in 33-way partitions of the one element set [18]. We note that the algebra AA of section 6 is B⊗2B^{\otimes 2}. Consider the tensor

TN:=TB⊠N,T_{N}:=T_{B}^{\boxtimes N},

where we now identify the basis of 𝕂2N\mathbb{K}^{2^{N}} with subsets of the set with NN elements. Note that TNT_{N} encodes 33-way partitions of the set with NN elements. Let us fix N:=3​kN:=3k and the uniform probability distribution on the three entries of TBT_{B}. We obtain the sweet piece S​PN​TBSP_{N}{T_{B}} that is exactly equal to the tensor TNT_{N} from [72]. This sweet piece is also the tensor representing the degree one multiplication in the kk-th Veronese subalgebra of B⊗NB^{\otimes N}. The dimension of this Veronese subalgebra equals twice the size of the sweet piece plus two. Combining this observation with [72]*Corollary 1.12 we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 6.5.

If the asymptotic rank of a sweet piece coming from tensors with minimal border rank has minimal asymptotic rank or if Veronese subalgebras of smoothable algebras give rise to tensors of minimal asymptotic rank, then the set covering conjecture from [36] is false.

We note that by [72]*Corollary 1.12 one does not need exponential improvements in the border rank of the tensors TNT_{N} to disprove the set covering conjecture. The obvious bound is 8k8^{k}, while the current best known bound is 12​8k\frac{1}{2}8^{k} [72]*p. 4, point (4). In fact, it would be enough to prove that asymptotic rank is at most

2⋅8k9⋅k.\frac{2\cdot 8^{k}}{9\cdot k}.

Below we provide a modest improvement on the upper bound.

Proposition 6.5.

The rank of the tensor TNT_{N} is at most

12​8k−∑i=k+1⌊N/2⌋(N2​i).\frac{1}{2}8^{k}-\sum_{i=k+1}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}\binom{N}{2i}.
Proof.

We proceed similarly to section 6. We start with Tℤ2∈(𝕂2)⊗3T_{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}\in(\mathbb{K}^{2})^{\otimes 3} and note that TNT_{N} is a subtensor of the minimal rank tensor Tℤ2⊠NT_{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}^{\boxtimes N}. By the substitution method the rank of TNT_{N} is bounded by the number of sets obtained as the symmetric difference of two subsets of cardinality kk of a set of cardinality NN. We note that such subsets are always even and of cardinality at most 2​k2k. The bound follows. ∎
